Orientation · Chapter 0 · about 17 min

The Language of Mathematics

Proofs, quantifiers, sets and functions: the vocabulary every later chapter assumes, and how to read this guide.

In this chapter

How to use this guide

Each chapter has the same shape. It opens by rebuilding the undergraduate core from the definitions, because after fifteen years the definitions are what fade first. It then moves to the ideas that a first graduate course adds, and ends with open problems and recent results. The coloured tags on section headings tell you which layer you are in, so you can skim the core of a subject you remember well and slow down where it gets new.

There are no exercises. In their place are questions to hold in your head while reading, worked examples, figures you can manipulate, and pointers to applications. Since you write software for a living, some ideas are also shown as code, and the chapter on computation explains why a proof and a program are closer relatives than most degrees let on.

You do not need to read in order. Chapters 1 to 5 are the trunk. After that, follow your interest. The last chapter collects books, lecture series and projects for going further.

CoreWhat a proof is

Mathematics is the study of what follows necessarily from precise assumptions. A definition fixes the meaning of a word exactly. A theorem is a statement shown to follow from definitions and earlier theorems by a proof: a finite chain of steps, each justified by a rule of logic. A lemma is a small theorem used on the way to a bigger one, a corollary is an easy consequence, and a conjecture is a statement someone believes but nobody has proved.

The standards are harsh by the norms of every other discipline. A billion confirming cases prove nothing. The claim that n2+n+41 is always prime survives for n=0,1,…,39 and dies at n=40. The Pólya conjecture, about how many integers have an odd number of prime factors, first fails near 9×108. Evidence guides belief, but only proof settles a question.

Logical connectives and quantifiers

Statements are built from smaller ones using and (∧), or (∨, always inclusive), not (¬) and implies (⇒). The implication P⇒Q is false only when P is true and Q is false. In particular a false premise implies anything, which is why a single contradiction in a system of axioms would make every statement provable.

The implication P⇒Q is logically the same as its contrapositive ¬Q⇒¬P, and different from its converse Q⇒P. "If and only if" (⟺, often written iff) asserts both directions.

The real power comes from quantifiers: ∀ ("for all") and ∃ ("there exists"). Order matters:

∀x ∃y (y>x)versus∃y ∀x (y>x).

Over the integers the first says every number has a bigger one (true) and the second says some number is bigger than all numbers (false). Much of the difficulty of analysis is quantifier bookkeeping. To negate a quantified statement, flip every quantifier and negate the inside: ¬(∀x ∃y P)≡∃x ∀y ¬P.

In code Quantifiers are loops

A programmer already has the right intuition. ∀ is all(...), ∃ is any(...), and nesting order is loop order.

# for all x there exists y with y > x: y may depend on x
all(any(y > x for y in Y) for x in X)
# there exists y bigger than every x: one y must work for all
any(all(y > x for x in X) for y in Y)

The difference from code is that X and Y are usually infinite, so no machine can run the loop. A proof is a finite argument that the loop would return True.

Proof techniques

Almost every proof you will meet combines a handful of moves.

  • Direct proof. Assume P, unfold definitions, compute, arrive at Q.
  • Contrapositive. Prove ¬Q⇒¬P when that direction gives you more to work with.
  • Contradiction. Assume the claim is false and derive an impossibility. The classic is the irrationality of 2​: if 2​=a/b in lowest terms then a2=2b2, so a is even, so a2 is divisible by 4, so b is even too, contradicting lowest terms.
  • Induction. To prove P(n) for all natural numbers, prove P(0) and prove P(n)⇒P(n+1). Induction is recursion run forwards. Strong induction and structural induction (over trees, formulas, data types) are the same idea.
  • Construction and counterexample. An existence claim is proved by exhibiting the object. A universal claim is refuted by a single counterexample.
  • Pigeonhole, counting twice, extremal choice. Pick the smallest counterexample, the longest path, the maximal element, and squeeze it for information.

Example Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes

Suppose p1​,…,pk​ were all the primes. The number N=p1​p2​⋯pk​+1 leaves remainder 1 when divided by each pi​, so none of them divides it. But N>1 has some prime factor. That factor is a prime missing from the list. So no finite list is complete.

Notice the shape: a short construction, a use of an earlier fact (every integer above 1 has a prime factor), and no computation at all. Around 300 BCE this was already mathematics in the modern sense.

CoreSets, functions and relations

Modern mathematics is written in the language of sets. A set is a collection of objects, its elements. We write x∈A for membership and A⊆B when every element of A is in B. Sets are often described by a property: {x∈R:x2<2}.

Notation Meaning
N,Z,Q,R,C natural numbers, integers, rationals, reals, complex numbers
A∪B, A∩B, A∖B union, intersection, difference
A×B Cartesian product: all ordered pairs (a,b)
P(A) or 2A power set: the set of all subsets of A
∣A∣ cardinality, the number of elements
f:A→B a function from A (domain) to B (codomain)
a↦f(a) what the function does to an element
∑,∏ sum and product over an index set
:= "is defined to be"

A function f:A→B assigns to each element of A exactly one element of B. Three adjectives recur everywhere:

  • injective (one-to-one): different inputs give different outputs;
  • surjective (onto): every element of B is hit;
  • bijective: both, so f has an inverse and pairs the elements of A and B perfectly.

A relation on a set is any set of ordered pairs. Two kinds matter most.

Definition Equivalence relation

A relation ∼ on A that is reflexive (a∼a), symmetric (a∼b⇒b∼a) and transitive (a∼b, b∼c⇒a∼c). It chops A into disjoint equivalence classes, and the set of classes is the quotient A/∼.

Quotients are how mathematics builds new objects by declaring things equal. The rationals are pairs of integers where (a,b)∼(c,d) when ad=bc. Clock arithmetic is the integers where two numbers are equivalent when they differ by a multiple of 12. A torus is a square with opposite edges identified. You will see the pattern in every chapter: take something, decide what to ignore, pass to the quotient.

The other kind is an order: a relation ≤ that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. If any two elements are comparable it is a total order (like R), otherwise a partial order (like subsets under inclusion, or commits in a git history).

CoreStructure and structure-preserving maps

The single most useful organising idea in twentieth-century mathematics fits in one sentence: study sets with extra structure, together with the functions that preserve that structure.

Objects Structure Maps that preserve it
Groups a multiplication with inverses homomorphisms
Vector spaces addition and scaling linear maps
Topological spaces a notion of nearness continuous maps
Smooth manifolds a notion of differentiability smooth maps
Measure spaces a notion of size measurable maps
Ordered sets an order monotone maps

Two objects are isomorphic when there is a structure-preserving bijection between them whose inverse also preserves structure. Isomorphic objects are the same for every purpose the theory cares about. A recurring game is classification: list all objects of some kind up to isomorphism. Finite-dimensional vector spaces are classified by one number, the dimension. Finite simple groups took a century and tens of thousands of journal pages. Smooth four-dimensional manifolds remain wild.

The pattern is so pervasive that it has its own theory, category theory, which appears in the computation chapter. If you have used interfaces, generics or functors in a typed language, you have met its shadow.

Intuition Abstraction is compression

A theorem about groups is proved once and applies to symmetries of crystals, to modular arithmetic, to elliptic curves and to Rubik's cube. Abstraction in mathematics does the job that a well-chosen interface does in software: it names exactly the assumptions an argument uses, so the argument can be reused wherever those assumptions hold.

CoreA short history of rigour

The Greeks invented proof and the axiomatic method. Euclid's Elements derived geometry from five postulates and stood as the model of certainty for two thousand years. Calculus, created by Newton and Leibniz in the 1600s, was spectacularly useful and logically shaky. It reasoned with infinitely small quantities that nobody could define. Bishop Berkeley mocked them as "ghosts of departed quantities", and he had a point.

The nineteenth century rebuilt everything. Cauchy and Weierstrass replaced infinitesimals with limits and the ε-δ definitions you met in analysis. Dedekind and Cantor constructed the real numbers out of rationals and, in doing so, discovered that infinity comes in sizes. Non-Euclidean geometry showed that Euclid's parallel postulate was a choice, and with that the idea of axioms as self-evident truths gave way to axioms as rules of a game. Around 1900, paradoxes in naive set theory forced a careful axiomatisation of sets, which the next chapter describes.

In 1900 David Hilbert gave a list of 23 problems that shaped the following century. In 2000 the Clay Mathematics Institute named seven Millennium Problems. One, the Poincaré conjecture, was proved by Grigori Perelman in 2003. The status of the rest, including some dramatic claims from 2026, is the subject of the frontiers chapter.

GradThe shape of the subject

A caricature that is still useful: mathematics has three ancient roots and one modern trunk.

  • Algebra studies operations and the structures they generate: equations, symmetry, number systems.
  • Analysis studies limits: continuity, change, approximation, infinite processes.
  • Geometry and topology study shape and space.
  • Foundations (logic and set theory) supply the common language.

The most celebrated results cross these borders. Fermat's Last Theorem is a statement about whole numbers whose proof runs through geometry (elliptic curves) and analysis (modular forms). The classification of surfaces is topology that is controlled by algebra. Quantum mechanics is linear algebra in infinitely many dimensions, which needs analysis to make sense. If one theme runs through this guide it is that the fields are projections of a single subject, and that the deepest insights are dictionaries between them.

Going deeper Three slogans to carry forward

Local to global. Understand something in small patches, then study the obstruction to gluing the patches together. Derivatives are local, integrals are global, and the fundamental theorem of calculus connects them. Cohomology is the general machine.

Linearise. Replace a hard nonlinear object by a linear approximation: tangent spaces, Lie algebras, representation theory, the Jacobian matrix in Newton's method.

Classify by invariants. Attach to each object a number, group or polynomial that does not change under isomorphism. If the invariants differ, the objects differ.

Foundations · Chapter 1 · about 17 min

Logic, Sets and Infinity

Sizes of infinity, the axioms everything rests on, and Gödel's discovery that proof has limits.

In this chapter

CoreCounting without numbers

Two sets have the same cardinality when there is a bijection between them. For finite sets this is ordinary counting. For infinite sets it is the only sensible definition, and it immediately does strange things. The even numbers can be paired with all natural numbers by n↦2n, so a set can have the same size as a proper part of itself. Dedekind took that as the definition of infinite.

A set is countable if it can be listed as a sequence a0​,a1​,a2​,…, that is, if it is in bijection with N (or is finite). The integers are countable: 0,1,−1,2,−2,… So are the rationals, by sweeping through the grid of fractions along diagonals. So is the set of all finite strings over a finite alphabet, and therefore the set of all computer programs and the set of all proofs. Countable infinity is written ℵ0​.

Theorem Cantor, 1874 and 1891

The real numbers are not countable.

The proof is the diagonal argument, among the most reused ideas in mathematics. Suppose the reals between 0 and 1 could be listed, and write each as an infinite decimal. Build a new number whose n-th digit differs from the n-th digit of the n-th number on the list (say, add 1 modulo 10, avoiding 9s to dodge the 0.0999…=0.1 ambiguity). The new number differs from every entry of the list in at least one digit, so it is not on the list. No list is complete.

The same argument proves the general statement: for any set A, the power set P(A) is strictly bigger than A. Given any f:A→P(A), the set D={a∈A:a∈/f(a)} cannot be f(d) for any d, because d∈D⟺d∈/f(d)=D. So there is no largest infinity: N, P(N), P(P(N)), and so on forever.

In code The diagonal is the halting problem

Replace "list of real numbers" by "list of all programs" and "digit n of number n" by "what program n does on input n". The diagonal argument becomes Turing's 1936 proof that no program can decide whether an arbitrary program halts. It also becomes the proof of Gödel's incompleteness theorem, and Russell's paradox is the same diagonal applied to "the set of all sets". One idea, four revolutions.

Since programs are countable and real numbers are not, almost every real number is uncomputable: no program prints its digits. The numbers we can name are a countable speck inside the continuum.

CoreThe axioms: ZFC

Cantor worked with a naive principle: any property defines a set. Bertrand Russell broke it in 1901 by asking about R={x:x∈/x}. Is R∈R? Either answer implies the other.

The repair, due to Zermelo and Fraenkel, is a list of axioms saying which sets exist. In ZFC everything is a set, and the axioms assert roughly the following.

  • Extensionality. Sets with the same elements are equal.
  • Pairing, union, power set. From given sets you may form {a,b}, unions and power sets.
  • Separation. From a set A you may carve out {x∈A:P(x)}. You may not form {x:P(x)} out of thin air, which blocks Russell.
  • Infinity. An infinite set exists.
  • Replacement. The image of a set under a definable function is a set.
  • Foundation. No infinite descending chains ⋯∈x2​∈x1​∈x0​.
  • Choice (the C). Given any family of nonempty sets, there is a function choosing one element from each.

Numbers are then implemented as sets, much as a high-level type is implemented in bytes: 0=∅, 1={0}, 2={0,1}, and in general n+1=n∪{n}. Ordered pairs are (a,b)={{a},{a,b}}, functions are sets of pairs, real numbers are sets of rationals. Nobody thinks about numbers this way day to day. The point is that one small axiom list suffices for essentially all of mathematics, so the consistency of everything reduces to the consistency of ZFC.

The axiom of choice

Choice is equivalent to Zorn's lemma (the form algebraists use) and to the statement that every set can be well-ordered. It is needed to prove that every vector space has a basis, that every ring has a maximal ideal, and that products of compact spaces are compact. It also has disturbing consequences.

Theorem Banach and Tarski, 1924

A solid ball in R3 can be cut into five pieces and the pieces reassembled, using only rotations and translations, into two balls each the same size as the original.

The pieces are not shapes in any ordinary sense. They are so scattered that they have no volume at all, which is how volume fails to be conserved. The theorem is the reason measure theory restricts attention to "measurable" sets, as the analysis chapter explains. Its real cause is algebraic: the group of rotations of 3-space contains a free group on two generators.

GradOrdinals and transfinite induction

Cardinals measure size. Ordinals measure position in a well-ordered sequence, and they let induction run past infinity. After 0,1,2,… comes ω, then ω+1,ω+2,…,ω⋅2,…,ω2,…,ωω,… Each ordinal is the set of all smaller ordinals. Ordinal arithmetic is not commutative: 1+ω=ω but ω+1>ω.

Ordinals are a precise measure of the strength of a recursion. A termination proof for a program is an assignment of ordinals to states that decreases at each step. Simple loops need ordinals below ω. Ackermann's function needs ωω. Proving that every Goodstein sequence reaches zero needs ε0​=ωωω⋅⋅, and the theorem is true but unprovable in Peano arithmetic. This "ordinal analysis" of theories is a living research area called proof theory.

GradGödel: the limits of proof

Hilbert's programme, around 1920, aimed to put all of mathematics on a formal basis and then prove, by safe finitary reasoning, that the system is consistent and complete. In 1931 the 25-year-old Kurt Gödel showed that this cannot be done.

Theorem Gödel's incompleteness theorems

Let T be a consistent theory whose axioms can be listed by a program and which can express basic arithmetic. Then

  1. there is a statement G in the language of T that T can neither prove nor refute;
  2. T cannot prove its own consistency.

The proof encodes formulas and proofs as numbers (the first compiler, in effect), so that arithmetic can talk about provability. A fixed-point construction then yields a sentence G that says "I am not provable in T". If T proved G it would prove something false. So G is unprovable, hence true. Incompleteness is not a defect of one system. Add G as an axiom and the new system has its own Gödel sentence.

Incompleteness does not mean that anything goes. Almost all working mathematics lives comfortably inside ZFC, and most of it needs far less. What it does mean is that some natural questions have no answer from the standard axioms.

Theorem The continuum hypothesis is independent of ZFC

The continuum hypothesis (CH) says there is no set whose size is strictly between that of N and that of R. Gödel (1940) showed ZFC cannot refute CH. Paul Cohen (1963) showed ZFC cannot prove it.

Cohen's method, forcing, builds new models of set theory by adjoining a carefully generic object to an existing one, a little like adjoining 2​ to the rationals. It opened a flood. Hundreds of statements in analysis, algebra and topology are now known to be independent of ZFC, among them the Whitehead problem about abelian groups and questions about the structure of the real line.

GradModel theory and the uses of logic

Logic is also a toolbox for ordinary mathematics. Model theory studies which structures satisfy which sentences. Its first theorem, compactness, says that if every finite subset of a set of first-order sentences has a model then the whole set does. Consequences include number systems with genuine infinitesimals (which finally made Leibniz's calculus rigorous, as nonstandard analysis) and slick proofs of facts in algebra, such as the Ax–Grothendieck theorem that an injective polynomial map Cn→Cn is surjective.

A key modern notion is o-minimality: a way of singling out "tame" families of sets that exclude pathologies like the graph of sin(1/x). It sounds like pure logic. It turned out to be the engine behind breakthroughs in number theory on how algebraic points sit inside transcendental shapes (the Pila–Wilkie counting theorem and the André–Oort conjecture). Jacob Tsimerman received a 2026 Fields Medal in large part for making o-minimality a standard method of arithmetic and complex algebraic geometry.

ResearchWhere research stands

New axioms and the fate of CH. If ZFC cannot decide CH, should we adopt axioms that do? One camp extends ZFC with large cardinal axioms, assertions that very large infinities exist (inaccessible, measurable, Woodin, supercompact cardinals). They form a hierarchy that calibrates the strength of every known natural theory, and they settle many questions about definable sets of reals, though not CH. Hugh Woodin's programme seeks an "ultimate L", a canonical universe compatible with all large cardinals, in which CH would hold. Others argue from forcing axioms that the continuum is ℵ2​. A third view, the multiverse, holds that there are many universes of sets and CH simply varies. Work published in 2024 and 2025 by Aguilera, Bagaria and Lücke introduced "exacting" and "ultraexacting" cardinals that fit awkwardly in the usual hierarchy and bear on which of these pictures is right.

Descriptive set theory and combinatorics. The study of definable sets (Borel, analytic, projective) now interacts with dynamics and graph theory. A striking example: Banach–Tarski-style "circle squaring" (cutting a disc into pieces that reassemble into a square) can be done with pieces that are Borel sets, hence measurable (Marks and Unger, 2017), with later work making the pieces progressively nicer.

Reverse mathematics. Which axioms does a given theorem actually need? Most classical theorems turn out to be equivalent, over a weak base theory, to one of five systems. The exceptions, especially around Ramsey's theorem for pairs, are an active topic that blends logic and computability.

Formalisation. The foundations of proof assistants are not set theory but type theory, with the same strength in different clothing. That story, and the surge of machine-checked mathematics in 2025 and 2026, is in the computation and frontiers chapters.

History A human note

Cantor's work was attacked by leading mathematicians of his day. Kronecker called him a corrupter of youth, and Cantor spent long periods in sanatoria. Hilbert defended him with a line that became famous: no one shall expel us from the paradise that Cantor has created. Gödel, for his part, became convinced late in life that CH is false and that the continuum has size ℵ2​.

The Trunk · Chapter 2 · about 19 min

Linear Algebra

Vector spaces, linear maps, eigenvalues and the singular value decomposition: the most widely used mathematics there is.

In this chapter

CoreWhy it is everywhere

Linear algebra is the part of mathematics we understand completely, and so the standard move in every other field is to reduce a problem to it. Calculus approximates curved things by linear ones. Differential equations are solved by diagonalising operators. Quantum states are vectors, observables are matrices. Search engines, recommendation systems, graphics pipelines, error-correcting codes and neural networks are all, at the bottom, multiplying matrices.

School linear algebra is about arrays of numbers. University linear algebra is about linear maps, with matrices as their coordinates. Getting that shift of viewpoint back is the main job of this section.

CoreVector spaces and linear maps

Definition Vector space

A vector space over a field F (think R or C) is a set V with an addition u+v and a scalar multiplication λv obeying the usual rules: addition is commutative and associative with a zero and negatives, and scaling distributes over both kinds of addition.

The examples go far beyond arrows in space: Rn; polynomials of degree at most d; all continuous functions on [0,1]; solutions of a linear differential equation; n×m matrices; bit strings of length n over the two-element field F2​.

A set of vectors spans V if every vector is a linear combination of them, and is linearly independent if no vector in the set is a combination of the others. A basis is a set that does both. Every basis of V has the same number of elements, the dimension of V. Choosing a basis identifies an n-dimensional space with Fn, but the choice is not canonical, and good linear algebra avoids choosing until it helps.

Definition Linear map

A function T:V→W with T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) and T(λv)=λT(v).

A linear map is determined by what it does to a basis. Record the images of the basis vectors of V as columns of coordinates in a basis of W and you have a matrix. Matrix multiplication is defined the way it is so that the matrix of a composition is the product of the matrices. That one sentence explains the row-times-column rule, why multiplication is associative and why it is not commutative.

Two subspaces come with every linear map: the kernel kerT={v:Tv=0} and the image imT. They are tied together by the first real theorem of the subject.

Theorem Rank–nullity

For T:V→W with V finite-dimensional, dimkerT+dimimT=dimV.

Read it as conservation of dimension: what the map does not crush, it faithfully embeds. It explains why n equations in n unknowns have a unique solution exactly when the homogeneous system has only the zero solution.

Determinants

The determinant of a square matrix is the factor by which the map scales signed volume. From that description the key properties are clear: det(AB)=detAdetB, a matrix is invertible iff det=0, and swapping two columns flips the sign. The formula with n! terms is a consequence that is useless for computing. Numerical code never computes a determinant to test invertibility.

Change of basis

If P is the matrix whose columns are a new basis, the same linear map is represented in the new basis by P−1AP. Matrices A and P−1AP are called similar. A large part of linear algebra asks: in which basis does this map look simplest?

CoreEigenvalues and diagonalisation

Definition Eigenvector

A nonzero vector v with Av=λv for a scalar λ, the eigenvalue. The map stretches v without turning it.

Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial det(A−λI). If V has a basis of eigenvectors, then in that basis A is diagonal, and everything about A becomes easy: Ak has diagonal entries λik​, and eAt has entries eλi​t. The long-run behaviour of the recurrence xk+1​=Axk​, or of the differential equation x′=Ax, is read off from the eigenvalues. Growth, decay and oscillation correspond to ∣λ∣ above 1, below 1, and complex λ.

Example Fibonacci by diagonalisation

The recurrence Fn+1​=Fn​+Fn−1​ is (Fn+1​Fn​​)=(11​10​)n(10​). The matrix has eigenvalues φ=21+5​​ and ψ=21−5​​. Diagonalising gives Binet's formula Fn​=(φn−ψn)/5​, and since ∣ψ∣<1, Fn​ is the nearest integer to φn/5​. Repeated squaring of the matrix computes Fn​ in O(logn) multiplications.

Not every matrix can be diagonalised. A shear (10​11​) has only one eigen-direction. Over C the best general statement is the Jordan normal form: every matrix is similar to a block-diagonal matrix whose blocks are an eigenvalue on the diagonal with 1s just above. Diagonalisable matrices are dense, so Jordan blocks are fragile, which is why numerical analysts distrust them and prefer the decompositions below.

CoreInner products and the spectral theorem

An inner product ⟨u,v⟩ adds geometry: length ∥v∥=⟨v,v⟩​, angle, and orthogonality. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality ∣⟨u,v⟩∣≤∥u∥∥v∥ is the most used inequality in mathematics. An orthonormal basis makes coordinates trivial to compute: the coefficient of ei​ in v is just ⟨v,ei​⟩. Gram–Schmidt turns any basis into an orthonormal one, and written in matrix form it is the QR factorisation.

Orthogonal projection onto a subspace gives the closest point in that subspace. That is the whole theory of least squares: to fit a model Ax≈b, project b onto the column space of A, which leads to the normal equations ATAx=ATb.

Theorem Spectral theorem

A real symmetric matrix (or complex Hermitian matrix) has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Equivalently A=QΛQT with Q orthogonal and Λ diagonal.

Symmetric matrices are everywhere: covariance matrices, Hessians, graph Laplacians, quantum observables, stiffness matrices. For all of them the spectral theorem says the map is a pure stretch along perpendicular axes. Try the Symmetric preset in the figure above and watch the dashed eigen-lines meet at a right angle.

CoreThe singular value decomposition

For a general, even rectangular, matrix the right generalisation is the SVD.

Theorem Singular value decomposition

Every real m×n matrix factors as A=UΣVT with U and V orthogonal and Σ diagonal with entries σ1​≥σ2​≥⋯≥0.

The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of ATA. The largest, σ1​, is the operator norm of A. The ratio σ1​/σn​ is the condition number, which measures how much solving Ax=b amplifies errors.

Theorem Eckart–Young

Keeping the top k singular values and vectors gives the best rank-k approximation of A in both the operator and Frobenius norms.

Application What the SVD does for a living

Principal component analysis is the SVD of a centred data matrix: the top singular vectors are the directions of greatest variance. Latent semantic indexing and early recommender systems are low-rank approximation. Image compression by truncated SVD is a classroom favourite. In signal processing, subspace methods such as MUSIC separate signal from noise by splitting the singular vectors of a covariance matrix. PageRank is the top eigenvector of the web's link matrix, and the Perron–Frobenius theorem guarantees it exists and is positive. LoRA fine-tuning of large language models freezes the weights and learns a low-rank update.

GradDuals, tensors and the coordinate-free view

The dual space V∗ is the space of linear maps V→F. In coordinates, vectors are columns and dual vectors (covectors) are rows. A linear map T:V→W induces a map backwards, T∗:W∗→V∗, which in coordinates is the transpose. A finite-dimensional space is isomorphic to its dual but not naturally so. An inner product is exactly a choice of such an isomorphism. This distinction between vectors and covectors is the origin of upper and lower indices in physics.

The tensor product V⊗W is the universal home for bilinear maps: a bilinear map out of V×W is the same as a linear map out of V⊗W. Its dimension is the product of the dimensions, which is why the state space of n qubits has dimension 2n and why quantum systems are hard to simulate. A matrix is an element of V∗⊗W. A "tensor" in machine-learning usage is an element of a tensor product of several spaces, written in a basis.

The exterior powers ΛkV are the antisymmetric tensors. The top one, ΛnV, is one-dimensional, and a linear map acts on it by a scalar. That scalar is the determinant, defined without choosing a basis. Exterior algebra returns in the geometry chapter as differential forms.

Going deeper Modules over a polynomial ring

A vector space with a chosen linear operator T is the same thing as a module over the polynomial ring F[x], where x acts as T. The classification of finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain then delivers Jordan normal form and the classification of finite abelian groups as two cases of a single theorem. This is the kind of unification that abstract algebra is for.

GradInfinite dimensions

Spaces of functions are infinite-dimensional, and the finite theory needs repair. Linear maps (now called operators) need not be continuous, the unit ball is no longer compact, and an operator can have no eigenvectors at all. The repaired theory is functional analysis. Its heroes are Hilbert spaces (complete inner product spaces), where the spectral theorem survives for self-adjoint operators with integrals over a continuous spectrum in place of sums. That is the mathematical framework of quantum mechanics, and of Fourier analysis, which has its own chapter.

ResearchWhere research stands

How fast can matrices be multiplied? The schoolbook method uses n3 multiplications. Strassen showed in 1969 that n2.81 suffices, by multiplying 2×2 matrices with 7 multiplications where the obvious count is 8. The exponent ω of the best possible algorithm is known only to lie between 2 and about 2.3713, after a string of small improvements through 2024. Whether ω=2 is open. The question is equivalent to finding the rank of a specific tensor, and tensor rank is NP-hard in general. In 2022 DeepMind's AlphaTensor found new small-case algorithms by reinforcement learning, and successors such as AlphaEvolve have kept trimming the constants.

Random matrices. Fill a large symmetric matrix with independent random entries and the histogram of its eigenvalues converges to Wigner's semicircle, whatever the entry distribution. Finer statistics, such as the spacing between adjacent eigenvalues, are also universal, and they match the observed spacings of zeros of the Riemann zeta function and of the energy levels of heavy nuclei. Proving universality (Erdős, Schlein, Yau, Tao, Vu and others, around 2010) was a landmark. Today random matrix theory underlies the analysis of high-dimensional statistics and of the loss landscapes of neural networks.

Numerical linear algebra at scale. Randomised algorithms (sketching, randomised SVD) now solve least-squares and low-rank problems on matrices too large to factor. The Kadison–Singer problem, a 1959 question from operator algebras, was resolved in 2013 by Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava using "interlacing families" of polynomials, with consequences for graph sparsification.

Compressed sensing and matrix completion. A sparse vector can be recovered from far fewer random linear measurements than its dimension (Candès, Romberg, Tao, Donoho, 2006), and a low-rank matrix from a small sample of its entries. Both rest on the geometry of high-dimensional convex sets.

History Where the words came from

Determinants (Leibniz, Seki, 1680s) are older than matrices. The word matrix is from Sylvester in 1850, and Cayley worked out matrix algebra a few years later. The abstract definition of a vector space is due to Peano in 1888 and was ignored for thirty years. Eigen is German for "own" or "characteristic", and the half-translated word eigenvalue stuck in English through Hilbert's school and quantum mechanics.

The Trunk · Chapter 3 · about 18 min

Real Analysis and Measure

Limits made rigorous, the real numbers, compactness, and the Lebesgue integral that modern probability and physics are built on.

In this chapter

CoreThe problem analysis solves

Calculus works. Analysis explains why, and finds the edge of the cliff. Can you swap a limit with an integral? Differentiate a series term by term? Is a continuous function always differentiable somewhere? (No: Weierstrass built one that is differentiable nowhere.) Eighteenth-century mathematicians answered such questions by instinct and sometimes got them wrong. The cure was a precise definition of limit and, underneath it, a precise definition of the real numbers.

CoreThe real numbers

The rationals have holes: the sequence 1,1.4,1.41,1.414,… wants to converge and has nowhere in Q to land. The reals fill the holes.

Definition Completeness

R is an ordered field in which every nonempty set that is bounded above has a least upper bound (supremum). Up to isomorphism it is the only one.

Completeness has several equivalent forms, each useful in different proofs: every bounded monotone sequence converges; every Cauchy sequence converges; nested closed intervals have a common point; every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence (Bolzano–Weierstrass). The reals can be constructed from Q as Dedekind cuts or as equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences. The second construction is a pattern, "completion", that also produces the p-adic numbers of number theory and the function spaces Lp.

CoreLimits and continuity

Definition Limit of a sequence

an​→L means: for every ε>0 there is an N such that ∣an​−L∣<ε for all n≥N.

Read it as a game. A sceptic names a tolerance ε. You must answer with a point N past which the sequence stays within tolerance forever. You win the limit if you have a strategy that beats every ε. The quantifier order ∀ε ∃N ∀n is the content.

Definition Continuity

f is continuous at a if for every ε>0 there is a δ>0 with ∣f(x)−f(a)∣<ε whenever ∣x−a∣<δ.

The big three theorems about continuous functions on a closed bounded interval [a,b] all depend on completeness:

  • Intermediate value theorem. f takes every value between f(a) and f(b).
  • Extreme value theorem. f attains a maximum and a minimum.
  • Uniform continuity. One δ works for all points at once.

Metric spaces and compactness

The definitions above use only the distance ∣x−y∣. A metric space is any set with a distance function satisfying the triangle inequality: Rn, the space of continuous functions with d(f,g)=max∣f−g∣, strings with edit distance, nodes of a graph. All of the limit vocabulary transfers.

Definition Compactness

A set K is compact if every cover of K by open sets has a finite subcover. In a metric space this is the same as: every sequence in K has a subsequence converging to a point of K.

Compactness is the most important definition in analysis and the hardest to motivate. Think of it as finiteness in disguise: a compact set behaves, for the purposes of continuity, like a finite set. Local information (a δ at each point) can be made global (one δ for all) because finitely many patches suffice. In Rn the compact sets are exactly the closed and bounded ones (Heine–Borel). In infinite dimensions that fails, and recovering some form of compactness is the central technical problem of the calculus of variations and PDE.

CoreDifferentiation, integration and their exchange

The derivative is the best linear approximation: f(a+h)=f(a)+f′(a)h+o(h). In several variables f′(a) becomes a linear map, the Jacobian matrix, and the chain rule says that derivatives compose by matrix multiplication. That statement is all of backpropagation.

The mean value theorem, f(b)−f(a)=f′(c)(b−a) for some c, converts information about f′ into information about f. Taylor's theorem extends it to polynomial approximation with an error term. The inverse function theorem says a smooth map with invertible derivative at a point is invertible near that point: linear algebra controls nonlinear behaviour locally.

The Riemann integral is the limit of sums of areas of thin rectangles, and the fundamental theorem of calculus says integration and differentiation undo each other.

Uniform convergence

A sequence of functions can converge at every point and still misbehave. The functions fn​(x)=xn on [0,1] are continuous, and their pointwise limit is 0 for x<1 and 1 at x=1, which is not. The fix is uniform convergence: supx​∣fn​(x)−f(x)∣→0. Uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous, and limits may be exchanged with integrals. This is why power series can be differentiated and integrated term by term inside their radius of convergence, and it is where the Fourier chapter picks up.

Theorem Stone–Weierstrass (the classical case)

Every continuous function on [a,b] is a uniform limit of polynomials.

So polynomials are dense in the continuous functions. The universal approximation theorems for neural networks are descendants of this result.

GradMeasure and the Lebesgue integral

The Riemann integral is too fragile for limits. The function that is 1 on rationals and 0 elsewhere is a pointwise limit of Riemann-integrable functions and is not itself Riemann integrable. Around 1902 Henri Lebesgue rebuilt integration, and his version is the one used in all modern analysis, probability and physics.

The idea is to slice the range of the function, not the domain. To integrate f, ask for each height y how large the set {x:f(x)>y} is. Lebesgue's analogy: to count a pile of coins, Riemann adds them up in the order they come, Lebesgue first sorts them by denomination.

Definition Measure

A σ-algebra on a set X is a collection of subsets closed under complements and countable unions. A measure μ assigns to each set in the collection a number in [0,∞], with μ(∅)=0 and μ(⋃Ai​)=∑μ(Ai​) for countably many disjoint sets.

Lebesgue measure on Rn extends length, area and volume to an enormous class of sets. It cannot be extended to all sets (given the axiom of choice), which is the lesson of Banach–Tarski. A set of measure zero is negligible, and a property that holds outside such a set holds almost everywhere. The rationals have measure zero. So does the Cantor set, though it is uncountable.

The payoff is a set of clean theorems for exchanging limits and integrals.

Theorem Dominated convergence

If fn​→f almost everywhere and ∣fn​∣≤g for a single integrable g, then ∫fn​→∫f.

Together with the monotone convergence theorem and Fubini's theorem (iterated integrals may be swapped for integrable functions), this is the working toolkit. A probability space is simply a measure space of total mass 1, a random variable is a measurable function, and expectation is the Lebesgue integral. Kolmogorov made that identification in 1933 and probability became a branch of analysis.

Lp spaces

For 1≤p≤∞, the space Lp consists of functions with ∥f∥p​=(∫∣f∣p)1/p<∞, where functions equal almost everywhere are identified. These are complete normed spaces (Banach spaces), and L2 is a Hilbert space with inner product ⟨f,g⟩=∫fgˉ​. Completeness is exactly what the Riemann integral could not deliver. Hölder's inequality ∥fg∥1​≤∥f∥p​∥g∥q​ for p1​+q1​=1 generalises Cauchy–Schwarz.

GradFunctional analysis in one page

Functional analysis is linear algebra for infinite-dimensional spaces with a topology. Four theorems carry most of the weight.

  • Hahn–Banach. There are enough continuous linear functionals to separate points from closed convex sets. Duality in optimisation rests on this.
  • Uniform boundedness. A pointwise-bounded family of operators on a Banach space is uniformly bounded. It gives a soft proof that some continuous function has a divergent Fourier series.
  • Open mapping and closed graph. A bounded linear bijection between Banach spaces has a bounded inverse.
  • Banach–Alaoglu. The unit ball of a dual space is compact in the weak-* topology. This is the replacement for Heine–Borel, and is how minimisers are shown to exist.

Distributions (Schwartz, 1940s) extend the notion of function so that everything can be differentiated. The Dirac delta, which physicists and engineers had used for decades, becomes a legitimate object: the linear functional ϕ↦ϕ(0). Sobolev spaces measure how many derivatives a function has in Lp, and are the natural setting for PDE.

GradFractals and geometric measure theory

Hausdorff dimension assigns a real-valued dimension to any set by asking how the number of small balls needed to cover it scales with their radius. The Cantor set has dimension log2/log3≈0.63, the Koch curve log4/log3≈1.26, a typical Brownian path in the plane has dimension 2. Geometric measure theory uses such tools to study surfaces with singularities, such as soap films.

ResearchWhere research stands

Frontier The Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions

A Kakeya set contains a unit line segment in every direction. Besicovitch showed in 1919 that such sets can have measure zero. The Kakeya conjecture says they must nevertheless have full dimension n in Rn. The planar case was proved in 1971. In February 2025 Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl posted a 127-page proof for R3, a problem that had resisted Bourgain, Wolff, Katz, Tao and many others, and Wang received a Fields Medal in 2026. The conjecture sits at the bottom of a tower of open problems in Fourier analysis (restriction, Bochner–Riesz, local smoothing) about how waves travelling in different directions can pile up. Dimensions four and above remain open.

Optimal transport. Monge asked in 1781 for the cheapest way to move a pile of earth into a hole of the same volume. Kantorovich reformulated it as linear programming. The modern theory (Brenier, McCann, Villani, Figalli) turns the space of probability measures into a kind of infinite-dimensional Riemannian manifold. It now drives results in geometry, PDE, economics and machine learning, where Wasserstein distances and diffusion models are direct applications.

Calculus of variations and regularity. Do minimisers of energy functionals have to be smooth? Hilbert's 19th problem asked this, and De Giorgi and Nash answered yes for one equation in the 1950s. For systems, and for geometric objects like area-minimising surfaces, singularities can occur, and measuring the size of the singular set is a deep current topic.

Harmonic analysis. Beyond Kakeya, 2025 brought a counterexample to the forty-year-old Mizohata–Takeuchi conjecture by Hannah Cairo, then 17. The Fourier chapter says more.

The metric geometry of data. Concentration of measure, the fact that well-behaved functions on high-dimensional spaces are nearly constant, explains why high-dimensional statistics works at all. It began in the functional analysis of Banach spaces (Milman, Talagrand) and is now core machine-learning theory.

History The arithmetisation of analysis

Cauchy's 1821 Cours d'analyse introduced limits but contained a famous mistake, a "proof" that a convergent series of continuous functions is continuous. Abel pointed to Fourier series as counterexamples, and untangling the error produced the concept of uniform convergence. Weierstrass's lectures in Berlin in the 1860s set the ε-δ style that every analysis course still uses. He published little. His students' notes spread the gospel.

PreviousLinear AlgebraNextComplex Analysis

The Trunk · Chapter 4 · about 18 min

Complex Analysis

Calculus over the complex numbers, where one derivative implies infinitely many and integrals are computed by counting poles.

In this chapter

CoreA subject where everything works

Real analysis is a zoo of counterexamples. Complex analysis is the opposite. Ask only that a function f:C→C have a derivative in the complex sense and it follows that f has derivatives of all orders, equals its Taylor series, is determined everywhere by its values on any tiny arc, and has integrals that can be evaluated by inspection. The rigidity is what makes the subject both beautiful and useful. It is the working language of signal processing, fluid dynamics, quantum field theory and, above all, the study of prime numbers.

CoreComplex numbers as geometry

A complex number z=x+iy is a point in the plane. In polar form z=reiθ, where Euler's formula eiθ=cosθ+isinθ packages all of trigonometry. Multiplying by reiθ scales by r and rotates by θ. So complex multiplication is the geometry of rotations and scalings of the plane, and i2=−1 is the unremarkable fact that two quarter turns make a half turn.

Theorem Fundamental theorem of algebra

Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root. So a polynomial of degree n factors completely into n linear factors.

The reals needed one extra number, i, to solve x2+1=0, and then no more are ever needed. Every proof of this theorem uses some analysis or topology. One elegant version: as z runs around a huge circle, p(z)≈zn winds n times around the origin. Shrink the circle to a point and the winding number must drop to 0. It can change only when the image curve crosses the origin, that is, when p has a root.

CoreHolomorphic functions

Definition Holomorphic

f is holomorphic on an open set if the limit f′(z)=limh→0​hf(z+h)−f(z)​ exists at every point, where h approaches 0 through complex values.

The limit must be the same from every direction, which is a far stronger demand than real differentiability. Writing f=u+iv and comparing the horizontal and vertical approaches gives the Cauchy–Riemann equations

∂x∂u​=∂y∂v​,∂y∂u​=−∂x∂v​.

Geometrically, the derivative of f as a map of the plane is a 2×2 matrix, and the equations force that matrix to be a rotation composed with a scaling. So a holomorphic map with f′=0 is conformal: it preserves angles and sends tiny circles to tiny circles. A second consequence: u and v are harmonic, meaning they satisfy Laplace's equation uxx​+uyy​=0. Every problem about steady-state heat, electrostatics or ideal fluid flow in two dimensions is a problem about holomorphic functions.

CoreCauchy's theorem and its consequences

Integrate a complex function along a curve γ in the plane: ∫γ​f(z)dz.

Theorem Cauchy's theorem

If f is holomorphic on and inside a closed curve γ, then ∮γ​f(z)dz=0.

Theorem Cauchy's integral formula

With the same hypotheses, for any point a inside γ,

f(a)=2πi1​∮γ​z−af(z)​dz.

The values of f on a loop determine its values everywhere inside. Differentiating under the integral sign shows f has derivatives of every order, and expanding z−a1​ as a geometric series shows f equals its Taylor series on any disc where it is holomorphic. A cascade of rigidity theorems follows.

  • Liouville. A bounded holomorphic function on all of C is constant. (This gives a two-line proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra: if p had no root, 1/p would be bounded and entire.)
  • Identity theorem. Two holomorphic functions that agree on a set with a limit point agree everywhere on a connected domain.
  • Maximum modulus. ∣f∣ has no interior local maximum unless f is constant.

Singularities and residues

Functions like 1/z are holomorphic except at isolated points. Near such a point a a function has a Laurent series ∑n=−∞∞​cn​(z−a)n. The singularity is a pole if only finitely many negative powers appear, and essential otherwise. Near an essential singularity the function takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often (Picard). Choose exp(1/z) in the figure above to see what that looks like.

The coefficient c−1​ is the residue. It is the only term that survives integration around a small loop, because ∮zndz=0 unless n=−1, when it is 2πi.

Theorem Residue theorem

∮γ​f(z)dz=2πipoles a inside γ∑​Resz=a​f.

Real integrals that defeat every substitution fall to this method. So do sums of series, inverse Laplace transforms and asymptotic estimates.

Application Poles, filters and stability

An engineer analysing a linear system takes its Laplace transform (or z-transform, for sampled signals) and obtains a rational transfer function H(s). The system is stable exactly when every pole lies in the left half-plane (or inside the unit circle for the z-transform). The frequency response is H evaluated along the imaginary axis (or unit circle), so poles near that line are resonances and zeros near it are notches. Filter design is the art of placing poles and zeros. The Nyquist stability criterion is the argument principle, which counts zeros minus poles inside a contour by the winding number of the image curve.

CoreConformal maps and the Riemann sphere

Add a single point ∞ to the plane and it closes up into the Riemann sphere, on which 1/z is a perfectly good function swapping 0 and ∞. The Möbius transformations z↦cz+daz+b​ are exactly the conformal bijections of the sphere. They send circles and lines to circles and lines, and they form the group PSL2​(C), which is also the group of Lorentz transformations of special relativity and the isometry group of hyperbolic 3-space.

Theorem Riemann mapping theorem

Every simply connected open subset of C, other than C itself, can be mapped conformally and bijectively onto the open unit disc.

However jagged the region, it is conformally the same as a disc. Since Laplace's equation is preserved by conformal maps, a boundary-value problem on a complicated region can be transported to the disc, solved there by an explicit formula, and carried back. The Joukowski map z↦z+1/z turns a circle into an aerofoil shape, and early aerodynamics computed lift this way.

GradAnalytic continuation and Riemann surfaces

Because a holomorphic function is determined by its values near one point, a function defined by a formula on a small region may extend, uniquely, to a much larger one. The series ∑zn converges only for ∣z∣<1 but the function it defines, 1−z1​, makes sense everywhere except z=1. The famous "identity" 1+2+3+⋯=−121​ is the true statement ζ(−1)=−121​ about the analytic continuation of ζ(s)=∑n−s, a series that converges only for Res>1.

Continuation around a singularity can return a different value: follow z​ once around the origin and it comes back as −z​. Riemann's resolution was to let the function live on a new surface that covers the plane several times, a Riemann surface, on which it becomes single-valued. The surface for z​ is two sheets glued along a cut. The surface for z3−z​ is a torus, which is the first glimpse of elliptic curves.

Compact Riemann surfaces are the same thing as smooth complex algebraic curves, and they are classified topologically by their genus g, the number of holes. The uniformisation theorem (Poincaré and Koebe, 1907) says every Riemann surface is a quotient of exactly one of three models: the sphere (genus 0, positive curvature), the plane (genus 1, flat) or the hyperbolic disc (genus 2 and above, negative curvature). Analysis, algebra, topology and geometry all meet in that one theorem.

GradSpecial functions that run number theory

The gamma function Γ(s)=∫0∞​ts−1e−tdt extends the factorial, with Γ(n)=(n−1)!. The Riemann zeta function ζ(s)=∑n≥1​n−s=∏p​(1−p−s)−1 encodes the primes in its Euler product, continues to the whole plane with one pole at s=1, and satisfies a functional equation relating s to 1−s. The location of its zeros governs the distribution of primes. The number theory chapter takes up that story.

Modular forms are holomorphic functions on the upper half-plane H that transform in a prescribed way under z↦cz+daz+b​ with integer a,b,c,d and ad−bc=1. They look like a curiosity. They turn out to be generating functions for an astonishing range of arithmetic data: numbers of representations as sums of squares, partition numbers, point counts on elliptic curves, and dimensions of representations of the Monster group.

GradSeveral complex variables

In two or more complex variables new phenomena appear. Hartogs' theorem says a holomorphic function cannot have an isolated singularity: a function holomorphic on a shell extends to the solid ball. Not every domain is a natural domain of existence for some function, and characterising those that are (pseudoconvexity, the Levi problem) shaped the subject. Complex manifolds and their cohomology lead into algebraic geometry and Hodge theory.

ResearchWhere research stands

Random conformal geometry. Many two-dimensional models of statistical physics at their critical temperature are believed to be conformally invariant in the scaling limit. Oded Schramm's 1999 insight was to describe the resulting random curves by Loewner's differential equation driven by Brownian motion: Schramm–Loewner evolution. It led to Fields Medals for Werner (2006), Smirnov (2010) and Duminil-Copin (2022). Current work connects SLE to Liouville quantum gravity, a theory of random surfaces, and has made parts of two-dimensional conformal field theory rigorous, including a proof of the DOZZ formula by Kupiainen, Rhodes and Vargas.

Hyperbolic surfaces and their spectra. A Riemann surface of genus at least 2 carries a hyperbolic metric, and the space of all such metrics is moduli space. Maryam Mirzakhani computed its volumes and used them to count closed geodesics. Building on her methods, Nalini Anantharaman and Laura Monk proved in 2025 that a random hyperbolic surface of large genus has, with probability tending to 1, a spectral gap as large as theoretically possible, the surface analogue of an optimal expander graph.

Complex dynamics. Iterate z↦z2+c and the set of c for which the orbit of 0 stays bounded is the Mandelbrot set. Whether it is locally connected (the MLC conjecture) is the central open problem. It would imply that hyperbolic dynamics is dense in the quadratic family. Progress comes from renormalisation theory.

Teichmüller theory and inter-universal claims. Shinichi Mochizuki's proposed proof of the abc conjecture builds on a far-reaching reworking of Teichmüller theory. It has not been accepted by the wider community, and the dispute is described in the number theory chapter.

History Riemann's eight pages

Bernhard Riemann's 1851 thesis introduced Riemann surfaces and the mapping theorem. His 1859 paper on the zeta function, eight pages long and his only work on number theory, stated the Riemann hypothesis in passing, as something "very likely" that he had set aside after "a few fleeting attempts". He died of tuberculosis at 39.

PreviousReal Analysis and MeasureNextAbstract Algebra

The Trunk · Chapter 5 · about 21 min

Abstract Algebra

Groups, rings and fields: the mathematics of symmetry and of number systems, up to Galois theory and representations.

In this chapter

CoreFrom solving equations to studying structure

For most of history algebra meant solving polynomial equations. The quadratic formula is Babylonian. Formulas for cubics and quartics were found in Renaissance Italy. Then nothing, for three centuries, on the quintic. In the 1820s Abel proved no formula exists, and Évariste Galois, before dying in a duel at 20, explained why by attaching to each equation its group of symmetries. The centre of gravity of algebra moved from equations to the structures behind them, and it has stayed there.

CoreGroups

Definition Group

A set G with an operation G×G→G that is associative, has an identity element e, and in which every element has an inverse. If also ab=ba for all elements, the group is abelian.

A group is what you get when you collect all the symmetries of something: the transformations that leave it looking the same, with composition as the operation.

  • (Z,+), and the integers mod n, written Z/n: the cyclic groups.
  • The symmetric group Sn​ of all n! permutations of n things.
  • The dihedral group Dn​ of the 2n symmetries of a regular n-gon.
  • Invertible n×n matrices GLn​(F), and its subgroups: rotations SO(n), unitary matrices U(n).
  • The nonzero elements of a field under multiplication.

A subgroup is a subset closed under the operation and inverses. A homomorphism φ:G→H satisfies φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b).

Theorem Lagrange

If H is a subgroup of a finite group G then ∣H∣ divides ∣G∣.

The proof is a picture: the cosets gH={gh:h∈H} are all the same size and tile G without overlap. Two quick consequences: a group of prime order must be cyclic, and a∣G∣=e for every element, which for the multiplicative group mod p is Fermat's little theorem ap−1≡1(modp), the fact RSA encryption is built on.

Quotients and the isomorphism theorem

When can the cosets of H themselves be multiplied to form a group? Exactly when H is normal: gHg−1=H for all g. The result is the quotient group G/H. Kernels of homomorphisms are normal subgroups, and conversely.

Theorem First isomorphism theorem

For a homomorphism φ:G→H, G/kerφ≅imφ.

This is rank–nullity for groups, and the same theorem holds for rings, modules and vector spaces. A group with no normal subgroups other than itself and {e} is simple. Simple groups are the primes of group theory: every finite group is assembled from simple ones (its composition factors), though unlike integers the assembly instructions are not unique.

Group actions

A group acts on a set X when each group element permutes X compatibly with the group operation. This is groups doing their job as symmetries. The orbit–stabiliser theorem says ∣orbit of x∣⋅∣stabiliser of x∣=∣G∣.

Example Counting necklaces

How many different necklaces can be made from 6 beads in 2 colours, if rotations of a necklace count as the same? Burnside's lemma says the number of orbits is the average number of colourings fixed by a group element. Rotation by k positions fixes 2gcd(k,6) colourings, so the answer is 61​(26+2+22+23+22+2)=14. The same lemma counts chemical isomers and distinct Rubik's cube patterns.

The Sylow theorems use actions to prove that if pk is the largest power of a prime dividing ∣G∣, then G has subgroups of order pk, they are all conjugate, and their number is ≡1(modp). They are the first serious tools for dissecting finite groups.

CoreRings and fields

Definition Ring and field

A ring has addition (forming an abelian group) and an associative multiplication that distributes over it. Rings here are commutative with a 1 unless stated. A field is a ring in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.

Rings to keep in mind: Z; polynomial rings F[x] and F[x1​,…,xn​]; the Gaussian integers Z[i]; Z/n; rings of functions on a space. Fields: Q,R,C; the finite fields Fp​=Z/p; rational functions F(x).

An ideal I is a subset closed under addition and under multiplication by any ring element. Ideals are to rings what normal subgroups are to groups: exactly the things you can quotient by. The quotient R/I is the ring R with every element of I declared to be zero.

Example Building new fields

R[x]/(x2+1) is the real polynomials with x2 declared equal to −1. It is C. Likewise F2​[x]/(x8+x4+x3+x+1) is a field with 256 elements, and its arithmetic is the byte arithmetic inside AES encryption. For every prime power q=pn there is exactly one field Fq​ with q elements, and there are no other finite fields.

An ideal P is prime if ab∈P implies a∈P or b∈P, and maximal if nothing lies strictly between it and R. Then R/P has no zero divisors and R/M is a field. In Z the prime ideals are generated by the prime numbers, which is where the name comes from.

Unique factorisation

In Z and in F[x] there is division with remainder, hence a Euclidean algorithm, hence every ideal is generated by one element (a principal ideal domain), hence unique factorisation into primes. The chain weakens as rings get more complicated. In Z[−5​],

6=2⋅3=(1+−5​)(1−−5​)

are two different factorisations into irreducibles. Kummer and Dedekind rescued uniqueness by factoring ideals instead of numbers, which is the origin of the word "ideal" and the start of algebraic number theory.

CoreGalois theory

Given a polynomial f over Q, adjoin its roots to obtain a field K, the splitting field. The Galois group Gal(K/Q) is the group of field automorphisms of K that fix Q. Each one permutes the roots of f, respecting every algebraic relation among them.

Theorem Fundamental theorem of Galois theory

There is an inclusion-reversing bijection between the subgroups of Gal(K/Q) and the fields between Q and K. Normal subgroups correspond to intermediate fields that are themselves splitting fields.

A problem about fields, which are infinite and slippery, becomes a problem about a finite group. The equation f=0 is solvable by radicals exactly when its Galois group is solvable, meaning it can be broken into abelian layers. The general quintic has Galois group S5​, whose only proper normal subgroup A5​ is simple and non-abelian. So there is no quintic formula. The same theory proves that an angle cannot be trisected and a cube cannot be doubled with ruler and compass, since constructible lengths live in towers of degree-2 extensions.

GradModules, and algebra over a ring

A module over a ring R is a "vector space" whose scalars come from R. Abelian groups are Z-modules, vector spaces with an operator are F[x]-modules, and representations of a group are modules over its group ring. Modules need not have bases, and how badly they fail to is measured by homological algebra: resolutions, Ext and Tor. Invented in topology, homological methods are now standard throughout algebra and geometry.

Commutative algebra, the study of commutative rings and their ideals, is the local theory behind algebraic geometry. Hilbert's basis theorem says every ideal in F[x1​,…,xn​] is finitely generated, so every system of polynomial equations is equivalent to a finite one. Gröbner bases make this algorithmic, a multivariable version of Gaussian elimination and the Euclidean algorithm at once, and are what computer algebra systems run when you ask them to solve polynomial systems.

GradRepresentation theory

A representation of a group G is a homomorphism G→GL(V): a way of making the abstract group act by matrices. The strategy is to study a group through all its linear shadows.

For a finite group over C, every representation is a direct sum of irreducible ones (Maschke), there are as many irreducibles as conjugacy classes, and each is determined by its character, the function g↦trρ(g). Characters of different irreducibles are orthogonal, so decomposing a representation is like computing Fourier coefficients. This is more than analogy. Fourier series are the representation theory of the circle group, and the discrete Fourier transform is the representation theory of Z/n.

Application Why physicists care

The symmetry group of a physical system acts on its space of states, so the states decompose into irreducible representations. Each irreducible is a multiplet of states with the same energy. The periodic table's shell structure comes from representations of the rotation group SO(3). Spin comes from its double cover SU(2). Quarks were predicted from the representation theory of SU(3), and elementary particles are, by Wigner's definition, irreducible representations of the symmetry group of spacetime.

Lie groups and Lie algebras

A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold, such as SO(n) or SLn​(R): a continuous family of symmetries. Its Lie algebra is the tangent space at the identity, with a bracket [X,Y]=XY−YX recording the failure of commutativity to first order. The Lie algebra is a linear object that captures almost everything about the group.

Killing and Cartan classified the simple Lie algebras over C: four infinite families An​,Bn​,Cn​,Dn​ (corresponding to SL, odd SO, symplectic and even SO) and five exceptions G2​,F4​,E6​,E7​,E8​. The classification is encoded in Dynkin diagrams, small graphs that reappear in the classification of singularities, quivers, regular polytopes and more, a pattern nobody fully understands.

GradThe classification of finite simple groups

Theorem Classification (completed around 2004)

Every finite simple group is one of: a cyclic group of prime order; an alternating group An​ with n≥5; a group of Lie type over a finite field (16 families); or one of 26 sporadic groups.

The proof spans roughly ten thousand pages by a hundred authors. A second-generation proof, more organised, is still being published volume by volume. The largest sporadic group, the Monster, has about 8×1053 elements and its smallest faithful representation has dimension 196,883. In 1978 John McKay noticed that 196,884, one more, is a coefficient of the modular j-function from complex analysis. This "monstrous moonshine" was proved by Borcherds in 1992 using vertex algebras from string theory.

ResearchWhere research stands

Frontier The Jacobian conjecture falls in dimension three

A polynomial map F:Cn→Cn whose Jacobian determinant is a nonzero constant is locally invertible everywhere. Ott-Heinrich Keller asked in 1939 whether it must then have a polynomial inverse. The question appeared on Steve Smale's list of problems for the 21st century and absorbed a long line of flawed proofs. In July 2026 Levent Alpöge announced an explicit counterexample in three variables, of degree 7, found with the AI model Claude Fable 5: a map with constant Jacobian that sends three different points to the same place. Because the example is short, anyone can check it by direct computation, and the frontiers chapter shows how. The two-variable case is still open.

Local-global conjectures for finite groups. John McKay's 1971 conjecture says that the number of irreducible characters of G of degree not divisible by p equals the same count for the normaliser of a Sylow p-subgroup, a far smaller group. Marc Cabanes and Britta Späth completed the proof in 2023 and 2024 through a decades-long reduction to simple groups. Stronger relatives (the Alperin weight and Dade conjectures) remain open.

Geometric representation theory. Representations are increasingly constructed from the geometry of spaces attached to a group: flag varieties, sheaves, and categories. The geometric Langlands conjecture, proved in 2024 by Gaitsgory, Raskin and seven co-authors across more than 800 pages, is an equivalence of two such categories attached to a Riemann surface and a group. It is a geometric cousin of the Langlands programme in number theory.

Groups as geometric objects. Geometric group theory studies an infinite group through the large-scale shape of its Cayley graph. Gromov's hyperbolic groups and the resolution of Thurston's virtual Haken conjecture (Agol, Wise, 2012) came from this viewpoint. Whether every hyperbolic group is residually finite is a well-known open question.

Growth in groups and expanders. How quickly do products of a generating set fill up a finite group? Helfgott's 2008 theorem for SL2​(Fp​) started a theory of "approximate groups" (Breuillard, Green, Tao) with applications to expander graphs and sieve methods in number theory.

History Emmy Noether

Modern abstract algebra, the habit of studying rings and modules by their ideals and homomorphisms, is largely the creation of Emmy Noether in Göttingen in the 1920s. She also proved the theorem that every continuous symmetry of a physical system gives a conservation law. Barred from a paid position for years because she was a woman, and expelled in 1933 because she was Jewish, she ended her career at Bryn Mawr. Van der Waerden's textbook Moderne Algebra, based on her lectures, set the template every algebra course still follows.
