Branches · Chapter 6 · about 20 min

Number Theory

Primes, congruences, the zeta function, elliptic curves and the Langlands programme: the oldest questions and some of the newest answers.

In this chapter

CoreThe queen and her servants

Number theory asks questions a child can state about the integers and answers them with the most sophisticated machinery mathematics owns. Are there infinitely many primes p with p+2 also prime? Unknown. Is every even number above 2 a sum of two primes? Unknown. Does xn+yn=zn have positive integer solutions for n>2? No, and the proof took 350 years and used most of this guide.

For a long time it was the proudly useless field. Since the 1970s it secures essentially all digital communication.

CoreDivisibility and congruences

The Euclidean algorithm computes gcd(a,b) by repeated division with remainder and, run backwards, finds integers with ax+by=gcd(a,b) (Bézout's identity). From that follows Euclid's lemma (if a prime divides ab it divides a or b) and from that the fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer above 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way.

Gauss's notation a≡b(modn) means n divides a−b. Congruence classes form the ring Z/n. An element a has a multiplicative inverse mod n exactly when gcd(a,n)=1, and the algorithm finds it. So Z/p is a field when p is prime.

Theorem Three workhorses

Chinese remainder theorem. If m and n are coprime, Z/mn≅Z/m×Z/n. A number mod mn is the same as a pair of residues.

Fermat and Euler. If gcd(a,n)=1 then aφ(n)≡1(modn), where φ(n) counts residues coprime to n. For a prime, ap−1≡1.

Primitive roots. The multiplicative group of Z/p is cyclic: some g has powers hitting every nonzero residue.

Application RSA and Diffie–Hellman

RSA: choose large primes p,q and publish n=pq and an exponent e. Encrypt by m↦memodn. Decrypt with d≡e−1(modφ(n)), since med≡m by Euler's theorem. Computing d needs φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1), which needs the factorisation of n.

Diffie–Hellman: two parties publish ga and gb in a cyclic group and share the secret gab. Security rests on the difficulty of the discrete logarithm. Used in the group of an elliptic curve, this is what secures most TLS connections today.

Shor's algorithm factors and computes discrete logarithms efficiently on a quantum computer, which is why standards bodies are moving to lattice-based schemes. Their security rests on the hardness of finding short vectors in high-dimensional lattices, a problem from the geometry of numbers.

Quadratic reciprocity

Which numbers are squares mod p? Exactly half the nonzero residues. For odd primes p=q, Gauss's "golden theorem" relates two apparently unrelated questions.

Theorem Quadratic reciprocity

"p is a square mod q" and "q is a square mod p" have the same answer, unless both primes are ≡3(mod4), in which case the answers are opposite.

Gauss gave eight proofs. Hundreds are known. The search for the right generalisation to higher powers drove number theory for two centuries, through class field theory, and ends in the Langlands programme.

CoreThe distribution of primes

Primes thin out, but how fast? Write π(x) for the number of primes up to x.

Theorem Prime number theorem (Hadamard, de la Vallée Poussin, 1896)

π(x)∼lnxx​,and more preciselyπ(x)∼Li(x)=∫2x​lntdt​.

So near x about one number in lnx is prime. A random 300-digit number is prime with probability about 1 in 690.

The proof goes through complex analysis. Euler observed that unique factorisation is equivalent to the identity

ζ(s)=n=1∑∞​ns1​=p prime∏​1−p−s1​.

Riemann extended ζ to the whole complex plane and found an explicit formula expressing π(x) as Li(x) minus a sum of oscillating terms, one for each zero ρ of ζ. The zeros are the frequencies in the "music of the primes". The trivial zeros are at −2,−4,… All others lie in the critical strip 0≤Res≤1. The prime number theorem is equivalent to there being no zeros on the line Res=1.

Theorem The Riemann hypothesis (open since 1859)

Every nontrivial zero of ζ(s) has real part exactly 21​.

A zero with real part β contributes an error of size about xβ to the prime count. The hypothesis says the error is as small as it can be, about x​: the primes are as regular as a random sequence would be. More than 1013 zeros have been checked. Hundreds of theorems begin "assuming RH".

Dirichlet's theorem (1837): every arithmetic progression a,a+n,a+2n,… with gcd(a,n)=1 contains infinitely many primes. Its proof introduced L-functions, cousins of ζ twisted by characters of (Z/n)×, and the idea that arithmetic facts are encoded in analytic functions.

GradAlgebraic number theory

To study integer equations, enlarge the integers. A number field is a finite extension K of Q, such as Q(i) or Q(32​), and its ring of integers OK​ plays the role of Z. Fermat's claim that an odd prime is a sum of two squares iff p≡1(mod4) becomes the statement that such primes factor in Z[i]: p=(a+bi)(a−bi).

Unique factorisation of elements can fail in OK​, but every nonzero ideal factors uniquely into prime ideals. The failure for elements is measured by a finite abelian group, the class group. A rational prime p can stay prime in OK​, split into several primes, or ramify (acquire a repeated factor). The splitting pattern of p is controlled by a specific element of the Galois group, the Frobenius at p. Class field theory, the summit of early twentieth-century number theory, describes all extensions of K with abelian Galois group in terms of the arithmetic of K itself, and contains every classical reciprocity law.

The p-adic numbers

The reals complete Q using the usual absolute value. For each prime p there is another absolute value, in which a number is small when it is divisible by a high power of p. Completing with respect to it gives the field Qp​ of p-adic numbers: base-p expansions that extend infinitely to the left. In Q2​, the series 1+2+4+8+… converges to −1, exactly as two's-complement arithmetic says it should.

Hensel's lemma is Newton's method in Qp​: a solution mod p with nonvanishing derivative lifts uniquely to a p-adic solution. The local–global principle hopes that an equation has rational solutions iff it has real and p-adic solutions for every p. It is true for quadratic forms (Hasse–Minkowski) and false in general, and the obstruction to it is a central object of study.

GradElliptic curves and modular forms

An elliptic curve is a smooth cubic y2=x3+ax+b. Its points form an abelian group under the chord-and-tangent rule.

Theorem Mordell, 1922

The group E(Q) of rational points on an elliptic curve is finitely generated: E(Q)≅Zr⊕(finite group).

The rank r is mysterious. Counting points mod p for each prime gives numbers ap​=p+1−#E(Fp​), which are packaged into an L-function L(E,s). The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, a Millennium Problem, says r equals the order of vanishing of L(E,s) at s=1. It is known when that order is 0 or 1.

Theorem Modularity (Wiles, Taylor–Wiles 1995; Breuil, Conrad, Diamond, Taylor 2001)

For every elliptic curve over Q there is a modular form whose Fourier coefficients are the numbers ap​.

A geometric object and an analytic object, defined in different worlds, carry the same arithmetic data. Fermat's Last Theorem follows: a solution ap+bp=cp would give the curve y2=x(x−ap)(x+bp), which by work of Frey, Serre and Ribet is too strange to be modular.

Mordell also conjectured that a curve of genus at least 2 has only finitely many rational points. Gerd Faltings proved it in 1983 and later proved Lang's generalisation to subvarieties of abelian varieties. He received the 2026 Abel Prize for this body of work.

GradThe Langlands programme

In 1967 Robert Langlands, in a letter to André Weil, proposed a vast web of conjectures: to every n-dimensional representation of a Galois group there should correspond an automorphic form (a generalised modular form) for the group GLn​, with matching L-functions. For n=1 this is class field theory. For n=2 over Q it contains the modularity theorem. In general it predicts that the two great sources of L-functions, arithmetic geometry and harmonic analysis on Lie groups, produce the same functions.

Proved cases include function fields (Drinfeld, Laurent Lafforgue, Vincent Lafforgue), the local correspondence for GLn​ (Harris, Taylor, Henniart, Scholze), the fundamental lemma (Ngô), and the geometric version (Gaitsgory, Raskin and collaborators, 2024). The full conjecture for number fields is far out of reach and organises a large fraction of research in pure mathematics.

ResearchWhere research stands

Frontier The quasi-Riemann hypothesis (October 2026)

Among several hundred results that OpenAI released on 6 October 2026 from an internal AI model was a claimed proof that ζ(s) and all Dirichlet L-functions have no zeros with real part above 87​. Before this, no zero-free half-plane to the left of Res=1 was known. The classical zero-free regions pinch to nothing as the height grows. The claim also rules out Landau–Siegel zeros, hypothetical real zeros very close to 1 whose possible existence has been a technical obstacle since the 1930s.

Status as of mid-November 2026: human number theorists have unpacked the argument, independent re-derivations of the Landau–Siegel part have been posted by William Banks and Bryce Kerr, and Quanta reports that experts largely believe the shorter proof is correct. It has not been peer reviewed or fully formalised. This is not the Riemann hypothesis, which asks for 21​ in place of 87​.

Zeros and gaps, by hand. In 2024 Larry Guth and James Maynard gave the first improvement since 1940 to bounds on how many zeros can lie far from the critical line, sharpening what is known about primes in short intervals. Yitang Zhang's 2013 theorem that some gap size below 70 million occurs infinitely often between primes, improved by Maynard and the Polymath project to 246, remains the state of the art toward twin primes.

Diophantine geometry. The abc conjecture says that if a+b=c with coprime terms, then c is rarely much larger than the product of the distinct primes dividing abc. It would imply a great many results at once. Mochizuki's 2012 claimed proof was published in 2021 in a journal he edits, but Peter Scholze and Jakob Stix identified what they regard as an unfixable gap, and most experts consider the conjecture open. On firmer ground, the André–Oort conjecture on special points of Shimura varieties was completed in 2021 by Pila, Shankar and Tsimerman using o-minimality.

p-adic geometry. Peter Scholze's perfectoid spaces (2011) and his later work with Laurent Fargues recast the local Langlands correspondence as geometric Langlands on a curve built from p-adic numbers. With Dustin Clausen he has proposed condensed mathematics, new foundations in which topology and algebra mix cleanly. Part of it, the "liquid tensor experiment", was checked in the Lean proof assistant in 2022.

Statistics of arithmetic objects. Manjul Bhargava and collaborators showed that the average rank of elliptic curves is less than 1 and that a positive proportion satisfy BSD. Whether ranks are bounded at all is debated. The record curve, found by Elkies and Klagsbrun in 2024, has rank at least 29.

Fermat's Last Theorem, machine-checked. A complete formal proof in Lean was announced in September 2026, the output of AI agents building on a multi-year human project led by Kevin Buzzard. See the frontiers chapter.

History Gauss, at 24

The Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801) introduced congruence notation, proved quadratic reciprocity, classified binary quadratic forms, and showed the regular 17-gon is constructible. Gauss wrote that mathematics is the queen of the sciences and number theory the queen of mathematics. G. H. Hardy, in 1940, took pride that number theory had no warlike use. Within a few decades it became the basis of military and commercial cryptography.

Branches · Chapter 7 · about 19 min

Topology

The study of shape without distance: continuity, surfaces, holes, knots, and the algebra that detects them.

In this chapter

CoreRubber-sheet geometry

Topology studies the properties of a shape that survive stretching and bending but not tearing or gluing. A circle and a square are the same. A sphere and a torus are different, because of the hole. A coffee mug and a doughnut are, famously, the same. What is left when you forget lengths and angles is the way a space is connected, and that turns out to control a surprising amount: whether a differential equation has a solution, whether a vector field must vanish somewhere, whether a robot arm can move between two configurations, whether a material conducts on its surface.

CoreTopological spaces

Continuity in a metric space can be phrased with no mention of distance: f is continuous iff the preimage of every open set is open. So keep the open sets and throw the metric away.

Definition Topological space

A set X with a collection of subsets called open, containing ∅ and X, and closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. A map is continuous if preimages of open sets are open. A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse.

This minimal definition covers Rn, surfaces, spaces of functions, the p-adic numbers, and stranger things such as the Zariski topology of algebraic geometry, where open sets are huge. The key properties are stated purely in terms of open sets:

  • Connected: not a union of two disjoint nonempty open sets.
  • Compact: every open cover has a finite subcover.
  • Hausdorff: distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods.

Continuous images of connected sets are connected (the intermediate value theorem, generalised) and of compact sets are compact (the extreme value theorem, generalised).

New spaces are built by products, subspaces and above all quotients: gluing. Take a square. Glue one pair of opposite edges to get a cylinder. Glue the other pair too and you get a torus. Reverse the direction of one gluing and you get a Klein bottle. Reverse both and you get the projective plane.

Theorem Classification of surfaces

Every compact connected surface without boundary is homeomorphic to exactly one of: the sphere with g≥0 handles attached (orientable, genus g), or the sphere with k≥1 Möbius bands sewn in (non-orientable).

Each has an Euler characteristic χ=V−E+F, computed from any triangulation and independent of it. For the sphere χ=2, which is Euler's polyhedron formula. For the genus-g surface χ=2−2g. A complete classification by one number and one bit is as good as mathematics gets.

CoreThe fundamental group

How do you prove a sphere is not a torus? Find an invariant. Fix a base point and consider loops that start and end there. Two loops are homotopic if one can be continuously deformed into the other. Loops can be composed by running one after the other, and homotopy classes of loops form a group, the fundamental group π1​(X).

  • On a sphere every loop shrinks to a point: π1​(S2) is trivial. Such spaces are simply connected.
  • On a circle a loop is classified by how many times it winds: π1​(S1)≅Z.
  • On a torus, π1​≅Z×Z: wind around the hole and through it, in either order.
  • On a figure-eight, π1​ is the free group on two generators, which is non-abelian: ab=ba.

A continuous map induces a homomorphism of fundamental groups, so π1​ is a functor from spaces to groups. That turns impossibility questions in topology into algebra.

Theorem Brouwer fixed point theorem

Every continuous map from a closed disc to itself has a fixed point.

Sketch for the 2-disc: if f had no fixed point, follow the ray from f(x) through x to the boundary. That defines a continuous retraction of the disc onto its boundary circle. Passing to π1​ would factor the identity map of Z through the trivial group, which is absurd. Brouwer's theorem and its relative, Kakutani's, are how Nash proved that equilibria exist in games.

The fundamental group is closely tied to covering spaces: the real line covers the circle by t↦e2πit, wrapping infinitely often, and in general the connected covers of X correspond to subgroups of π1​(X). The correspondence is formally identical to the Galois correspondence. Grothendieck later made that identity precise, and the Galois group of Q is, in his language, the fundamental group of a point.

CoreHomology

Fundamental groups are hard to compute and see only one-dimensional loops. Homology is a cruder, computable invariant in every dimension. Triangulate the space. Let Ck​ be the formal sums of k-dimensional simplices, and let ∂:Ck​→Ck−1​ send each simplex to the alternating sum of its faces. The crucial fact is

∂∘∂=0(a boundary has no boundary).

So boundaries are cycles, and the k-th homology group measures the cycles that are not boundaries:

Hk​(X)=ker∂k​/im∂k+1​.

The rank of Hk​ is the Betti number bk​, the number of independent k-dimensional holes: b0​ counts connected pieces, b1​ counts loops, b2​ counts enclosed voids. The Euler characteristic is ∑(−1)kbk​. For the torus (b0​,b1​,b2​)=(1,2,1).

In code Homology is linear algebra

The boundary maps are integer matrices and computing homology is Gaussian elimination (Smith normal form). Topological data analysis applies this to point clouds: connect points closer than r, compute homology, and track which holes persist as r grows. Persistent homology has been used to find structure in neural recordings, cosmological surveys and the loss surfaces of neural networks. Libraries such as GUDHI and Ripser make it a few lines of Python.

CoreManifolds

A manifold of dimension n is a space that looks locally like Rn: curves, surfaces, the configuration space of a mechanism, spacetime. A smooth manifold comes with compatible local coordinate charts so that calculus makes sense on it. Smooth manifolds are the stage for the next chapter. Here are topological facts about them.

  • Hairy ball theorem. Every continuous tangent vector field on the 2-sphere vanishes somewhere. You cannot comb a hairy ball flat, and somewhere on Earth the horizontal wind speed is zero. More generally the zeros of a vector field, counted with signs, sum to the Euler characteristic (Poincaré–Hopf).
  • Poincaré duality. On a compact oriented n-manifold, bk​=bn−k​.
  • Jordan curve theorem. A simple closed curve in the plane has an inside and an outside. Obvious, and hard to prove.

GradCohomology, homotopy and beyond

Cohomology is homology dualised: Hk(X) consists of functions on cycles. It carries more structure, a product that makes H∗(X) a ring. On a smooth manifold it can be computed from differential forms (de Rham cohomology): closed forms modulo exact forms. The statement "a curl-free field on a simply connected region is a gradient" is H1=0.

Higher homotopy groups πn​(X) classify maps of the n-sphere into X. They are abelian for n≥2 and brutally hard to compute. The Hopf map shows π3​(S2)≅Z: the 3-sphere wraps around the 2-sphere in an essential way, with fibres that are linked circles. The groups πn+k​(Sn) stabilise as n grows to the stable homotopy groups of spheres, an irregular sequence (Z,Z/2,Z/2,Z/24,0,0,Z/2,Z/240,…) whose structure is a central problem of algebraic topology.

Fibre bundles are spaces that look locally like a product: the Möbius band is a twisted bundle of intervals over a circle. Characteristic classes are cohomology classes measuring the twist. In physics a gauge field is a connection on a bundle and its topological charge is a characteristic class.

Theorem Poincaré conjecture (Perelman, 2003)

A compact simply connected 3-manifold is homeomorphic to the 3-sphere.

Perelman in fact proved Thurston's geometrisation conjecture: every compact 3-manifold decomposes canonically into pieces each carrying one of eight geometries, most often hyperbolic. His tool was Hamilton's Ricci flow, a heat equation for metrics, so the hardest theorem of topology was proved with PDE. The higher-dimensional analogues had been proved earlier (Smale for n≥5, Freedman for n=4 topologically).

Dimension four is different

In dimensions 5 and above there is room to untangle things, and classification reduces to algebra. In dimensions 2 and 3 geometry takes over. Dimension 4 is the wild case. Donaldson (1983) used the Yang–Mills equations of particle physics to show that R4, alone among Euclidean spaces, has exotic smooth structures, in fact uncountably many. The smooth four-dimensional Poincaré conjecture, asking whether an exotic 4-sphere exists, is wide open.

Knots

A knot is a circle embedded in 3-space, up to deformation. Invariants distinguish them: the knot group π1​ of the complement, the Alexander polynomial, and the Jones polynomial (1984), which came from operator algebras and was explained by Witten using quantum field theory. Khovanov homology (1999) "categorifies" the Jones polynomial into a homology theory. Kronheimer and Mrowka proved in 2010 that it detects the unknot.

Application Topology in physics and engineering

The quantum Hall effect has conductance quantised to integer multiples of e2/h because the integer is a characteristic class (a Chern number) of a bundle over momentum space. Topological insulators and proposals for fault-tolerant topological quantum computing, where information is stored in the braiding of quasi-particles, extend the idea. In robotics, the "topological complexity" of a configuration space bounds how many discontinuities any motion planner must have.

ResearchWhere research stands

The Kervaire invariant problem, closed. In which dimensions can a framed manifold fail to be surgically converted into a sphere? Only dimensions of the form 2j−2 are possible. Examples were known in dimensions 2, 6, 14, 30 and 62. Hill, Hopkins and Ravenel showed in 2009 that none exist from 254 upward. In late 2024 Weinan Lin, Guozhen Wang and Zhouli Xu settled the last case with a large computer-assisted calculation: such manifolds do exist in dimension 126.

The telescope conjecture, refuted. Ravenel's 1984 conjectures described the large-scale structure of stable homotopy theory. All but one were proved in the 1980s. In 2023 Burklund, Hahn, Levy and Schlank disproved the last, the telescope conjecture, which implies the stable homotopy groups of spheres grow faster than had been expected.

Symplectic topology. John Pardon's 2026 Fields Medal recognised foundational work on counting holomorphic curves and on Fukaya categories, the algebraic structures behind mirror symmetry, alongside earlier results on knots and on group actions on 3-manifolds.

Low-dimensional surprises. In 2025 Brittenham and Hermiller found a pair of knots showing that the unknotting number is not additive under connected sum, overturning a conjecture nearly a century old. The search used computers heavily. Machine learning has also been used to conjecture new relations between knot invariants, later proved by hand.

Higher categories. Lurie's ∞-categories treat homotopies between homotopies, to all orders, as first-class data. They are now the working language of homotopy theory and derived algebraic geometry, and the basis of homotopy type theory, a foundation for mathematics in which equality itself has topological structure.

History From bridges to analysis situs

Euler's 1736 solution of the Königsberg bridges problem and his polyhedron formula are topology before the name. Poincaré founded the modern subject in Analysis Situs (1895), introducing the fundamental group and homology, and posing his conjecture in 1904 after noticing that his first guess was false. Emmy Noether pointed out in the 1920s that homology numbers should be regarded as groups, the step that made the subject algebraic.

Branches · Chapter 8 · about 18 min

Differential Geometry

Curvature, manifolds, differential forms and the geometry behind general relativity, mechanics and gauge theory.

In this chapter

CoreGeometry after Euclid

For two millennia geometry meant Euclid, and mathematicians tried to derive his fifth postulate, that through a point off a line there is exactly one parallel, from the other four. Around 1830 Gauss, Bolyai and Lobachevsky realised the attempts fail because there is a consistent geometry, hyperbolic geometry, with infinitely many parallels. Riemann's 1854 lecture then recast geometry entirely: a space is a manifold equipped with a rule for measuring infinitesimal lengths, and its curvature is a quantity that can vary from point to point. Sixty years later Einstein identified that curvature with gravity.

Differential geometry is calculus on curved spaces. It is the language of general relativity, classical mechanics, gauge theories of particle physics, and increasingly of statistics and machine learning.

CoreCurves and surfaces

A curve in space, parametrised by arc length, is described completely by two functions: curvature κ, how fast it turns, and torsion τ, how fast it twists out of its plane. A circle of radius r has κ=1/r.

For a surface in R3, slice through a point with planes containing the normal vector. Each slice is a curve with a curvature. The largest and smallest values are the principal curvatures k1​,k2​.

Definition Gaussian and mean curvature

K=k1​k2​ is the Gaussian curvature. H=21​(k1​+k2​) is the mean curvature.

Theorem Theorema Egregium (Gauss, 1827)

Gaussian curvature depends only on distances measured within the surface. It is unchanged by bending without stretching.

Gauss called it his "remarkable theorem". A flat sheet has K=0, so it can be rolled into a cylinder (K=0) but never into a piece of a sphere (K>0): every flat map of the Earth distorts distances. It is also why a pizza slice folded along its length stays rigid. Having curved it one way, the slice cannot droop the other way without making K=0.

Mean curvature, by contrast, depends on the embedding. Surfaces with H=0 are minimal surfaces, the shapes of soap films, which locally minimise area.

Theorem Gauss–Bonnet

For a compact surface S without boundary, ∫S​KdA=2πχ(S).

The left side is geometry: bend the surface and K changes at every point. The right side is topology: an integer that cannot change. However you dent a sphere, the total curvature is 4π. This is the prototype of the index theorems, which equate an analytic quantity with a topological one.

CoreManifolds and tangent spaces

To do geometry without an ambient space, we need intrinsic definitions. A smooth manifold M is covered by coordinate charts with smooth transition maps. At each point p there is a tangent space Tp​M, a vector space of the same dimension as M, whose elements are velocity vectors of curves through p, or equivalently directional derivative operators. A smooth map f:M→N has a derivative dfp​:Tp​M→Tf(p)​N, a linear map, which in coordinates is the Jacobian matrix. The tangent spaces fit together into the tangent bundle TM.

In code Automatic differentiation is differential geometry

Forward-mode autodiff propagates tangent vectors: it computes the pushforward df, composing Jacobian-vector products left to right. Reverse mode propagates covectors: it computes the pullback df∗ on cotangent spaces, composing vector-Jacobian products right to left. A scalar loss has a one-dimensional output, so one pullback gives the whole gradient. That is why backpropagation is reverse mode, and why JAX names its primitives jvp and vjp.

CoreDifferential forms and Stokes' theorem

A differential k-form is a thing that can be integrated over a k-dimensional oriented piece of a manifold: at each point it is an antisymmetric multilinear function of k tangent vectors. A 0-form is a function, a 1-form such as Pdx+Qdy is integrated along curves, a 2-form over surfaces. The exterior derivative d takes k-forms to (k+1)-forms and satisfies d∘d=0. In R3 it specialises to gradient, curl and divergence, and d2=0 is "curl of a gradient is zero" and "divergence of a curl is zero".

Theorem Stokes' theorem

For a (k−1)-form ω on an oriented k-dimensional manifold M with boundary ∂M,

∫M​dω=∫∂M​ω.

The fundamental theorem of calculus, Green's theorem, the divergence theorem and the classical Stokes theorem are all this one statement. It says d is the adjoint of the boundary operator ∂, which is why de Rham cohomology (closed forms modulo exact forms) computes the same numbers as the homology of the topology chapter.

Maxwell's equations, four vector equations in most textbooks, become two: dF=0 and d⋆F=J, where F is the electromagnetic 2-form on spacetime. The first says that F is locally dA for a potential A. Whether it is globally so depends on the topology of the region, which is the mathematics of the Aharonov–Bohm effect.

GradRiemannian geometry

A Riemannian metric g is a smoothly varying inner product on each tangent space. It defines lengths of curves, angles, volumes, and geodesics: curves that are locally shortest, the straight lines of the geometry.

To differentiate a vector field along a curve one needs to compare tangent spaces at different points. A connection supplies the rule, and there is a unique one compatible with the metric and without torsion, the Levi-Civita connection. It defines parallel transport. Carry a vector around a closed loop on a curved surface, keeping it "constant", and it comes back rotated. On a sphere, a vector carried around a triangle with three right angles returns turned by 90°.

The Riemann curvature tensor R records this failure infinitesimally: it measures how much parallel transport around a tiny parallelogram rotates vectors, or equivalently the failure of covariant derivatives to commute. Its contractions are the Ricci curvature (how volumes of small geodesic balls deviate from the Euclidean value) and the scalar curvature.

Application General relativity

Spacetime is a 4-manifold with a metric of signature (−,+,+,+). Freely falling bodies follow geodesics. The Einstein field equations

Rμν​−21​Rgμν​+Λgμν​=c48πG​Tμν​

say that Ricci curvature is determined by the density and flow of energy and momentum. Matter tells spacetime how to curve, and spacetime tells matter how to move. Black holes, gravitational waves and the expanding universe are particular solutions. The Schwarzschild solution was found within months of the theory, in 1916. That generic solutions develop singularities was proved by Penrose in 1965 using topology, work recognised with the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Curvature constrains topology. A complete manifold with Ricci curvature bounded below by a positive constant is compact with finite fundamental group (Myers). A simply connected complete manifold with nonpositive sectional curvature is diffeomorphic to Rn (Cartan–Hadamard). Comparison geometry (Gromov) extended such results to spaces far rougher than manifolds.

GradThree geometries of the twentieth century

Lie groups and symmetric spaces. Felix Klein's Erlangen programme (1872) defined a geometry as the study of invariants of a group action. Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic and projective geometry are the homogeneous spaces of different Lie groups.

Symplectic geometry. The phase space of a mechanical system, positions and momenta together, carries a closed non-degenerate 2-form ω=∑dpi​∧dqi​. Hamilton's equations say the system flows along the vector field that ω associates to the energy function. A symplectic manifold has no local invariants like curvature (Darboux): all the interest is global. Gromov's non-squeezing theorem (1985) says a ball in phase space cannot be symplectically squeezed into a thinner cylinder, a classical shadow of the uncertainty principle. His method of counting pseudo-holomorphic curves created modern symplectic topology.

Complex and Kähler geometry. A manifold with compatible Riemannian, symplectic and complex structures is Kähler. Smooth complex projective varieties are Kähler, so this is where differential geometry meets algebraic geometry. Calabi–Yau manifolds, Kähler manifolds with zero Ricci curvature whose existence Yau proved in 1976, are the extra dimensions of string theory. Mirror symmetry predicts that Calabi–Yau manifolds come in pairs with the complex geometry of one equivalent to the symplectic geometry of the other.

Gauge theory

A principal bundle attaches a copy of a Lie group G to each point of spacetime, a connection on it is a gauge field, and its curvature is the field strength. For G=U(1) this is electromagnetism. For SU(2)×U(1) and SU(3) it is the weak and strong forces: the Standard Model is a statement in differential geometry. The Yang–Mills equations generalise Maxwell's. Their solutions were used by Donaldson, and later Seiberg and Witten, to discover the exotic behaviour of four-dimensional manifolds. Showing that quantum Yang–Mills theory exists and has a mass gap is a Millennium Problem.

Theorem Atiyah–Singer index theorem (1963)

For an elliptic differential operator on a compact manifold, the number of independent solutions minus the number of independent constraints (the analytic index) equals a quantity computed from characteristic classes (the topological index).

Gauss–Bonnet and the Riemann–Roch theorem of algebraic geometry are special cases. In physics the theorem counts zero modes of the Dirac operator and explains anomalies in quantum field theory.

ResearchWhere research stands

Geometric flows. Evolve a shape by a heat-type equation and watch it improve. Ricci flow ∂t​g=−2Ric proved the Poincaré conjecture. Brendle and Schoen used it to prove the differentiable sphere theorem (2007), and work on four-dimensional Ricci flow with surgery is under way. Mean curvature flow moves a surface in the direction that decreases area fastest. Understanding its singularities, where necks pinch, is very active, including proofs of the mean convex neighbourhood conjecture (Choi, Haslhofer and Hershkovits) and the multiplicity-one conjecture (Bamler and Kleiner, 2023).

Minimal surfaces. Marques and Neves revived Almgren–Pitts min-max theory to prove the Willmore conjecture (2012), and together with Irie, Song and others showed that a generic closed manifold contains infinitely many minimal hypersurfaces, settling a question of Yau.

Scalar curvature and general relativity. The positive mass theorem (Schoen–Yau, Witten) says an isolated gravitating system has nonnegative total mass. Gromov has proposed a programme to understand spaces with scalar curvature bounded below. The stability of the Kerr black hole under small perturbations, proved for slow rotation by Klainerman, Szeftel and collaborators in 2022 in about 2,000 pages, is a major result in mathematical relativity.

Symplectic topology and mirror symmetry. Kontsevich's homological mirror symmetry conjecture (1994) equates the Fukaya category of one space with the derived category of sheaves on its mirror. Making Fukaya categories and curve counts rigorous in general required new foundations, an area in which John Pardon (Fields Medal 2026) has been central.

Information geometry and machine learning. A family of probability distributions is a manifold with a natural metric, the Fisher information. Natural-gradient methods, optimisation on manifolds, and "geometric deep learning", which builds symmetry and gauge-equivariance into network architectures, are applications that would have surprised Riemann less than one might think.

History Riemann's audition

Riemann's 1854 lecture "On the hypotheses which lie at the foundations of geometry" was his probationary lecture for a teaching post at Göttingen. He submitted three topics. Gauss, against custom, chose the third, the one Riemann had prepared least. The lecture defined manifolds, metrics and curvature in arbitrary dimensions and speculated that the geometry of physical space might be determined by the forces acting in it.

Branches · Chapter 9 · about 19 min

Differential Equations and Dynamics

How things change: ODEs, chaos, the great PDEs of physics, and the open question of whether fluids can blow up.

In this chapter

CoreLaws of change

Newton's insight was that nature's laws are easiest to state as relations between a quantity and its rates of change. A differential equation is such a relation, and a solution is a function satisfying it. Almost all of physics, and much of biology, chemistry, economics and engineering, is written this way.

Two kinds of question arise. The classical one: find a formula for the solution. That is rarely possible. The modern one, due to Poincaré: without solving, describe the qualitative behaviour of all solutions. Do they settle down, oscillate, or wander chaotically? Does a solution exist at all, and for how long?

CoreOrdinary differential equations

An ODE system has the form x′(t)=f(x(t)) with x(t)∈Rn. Think of f as a vector field, an arrow at each point of phase space, and of a solution as a path that follows the arrows.

Theorem Existence and uniqueness (Picard–Lindelöf)

If f is Lipschitz continuous, then through every initial point x(0)=x0​ there is exactly one solution, at least for a short time.

Uniqueness means trajectories in phase space never cross, which is the mathematical form of determinism. Both hypotheses matter. The equation x′=∣x∣​ has many solutions starting at 0. The equation x′=x2 with x(0)=1 has the solution 1−t1​, which blows up at t=1.

Linear systems

x′=Ax is solved by the matrix exponential x(t)=eAtx0​, and its behaviour is read from the eigenvalues of A: negative real parts give decay, positive give growth, imaginary parts give rotation.

For a nonlinear system, find the equilibria (where f=0) and linearise: the Jacobian of f at an equilibrium decides its stability. This is the "linearise" slogan at work. A Lyapunov function, a quantity that decreases along trajectories like energy under friction, proves stability without solving anything. In the plane, the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem says bounded trajectories can only approach equilibria or periodic orbits. Chaos needs three dimensions, or discrete time.

CoreChaos

The logistic map is the simplest system showing the essential features of chaos: deterministic rules, bounded motion, and sensitive dependence on initial conditions, so that nearby starting points separate exponentially fast. The rate of separation is the Lyapunov exponent. Prediction is possible only for a time proportional to the logarithm of the precision of the initial data. For weather the horizon is about two weeks, and no improvement in computers will change the logarithm.

Edward Lorenz met this in 1963 in a three-variable caricature of atmospheric convection:

x′=σ(y−x),y′=x(ρ−z)−y,z′=xy−βz.

Its trajectories settle onto a strange attractor, a fractal set of dimension about 2.06 on which the motion never repeats. That the Lorenz attractor really exists and is chaotic was proved rigorously only in 1999, by Warwick Tucker, using interval arithmetic: a computer-assisted proof.

Chaos is not disorder. Chaotic systems have precise statistical laws, studied by ergodic theory. A system is ergodic if time averages along almost every trajectory equal averages over space. Birkhoff's ergodic theorem makes that exact, and it is the assumption underneath statistical mechanics.

Going deeper Order inside chaos: KAM theory

The solar system is a perturbation of an exactly solvable system, since planets attract each other weakly compared with the Sun. Does the perturbation destroy stability? Kolmogorov, Arnold and Moser proved that most of the regular, quasi-periodic motions survive a small perturbation, specifically those whose frequency ratios are badly approximable by rationals. Resonant motions break up into chaotic zones. Number theory, in the form of Diophantine approximation, decides the fate of orbits. The gaps in the asteroid belt at resonances with Jupiter are the theorem made visible.

CoreThe great PDEs

A partial differential equation involves derivatives in several variables. Three linear equations are the archetypes. Here Δ=∂x1​2​+⋯+∂xn​2​ is the Laplacian, which measures how much a function at a point differs from its average nearby.

Equation Form Behaviour Models
Laplace (elliptic) Δu=0 equilibrium, as smooth as possible electrostatics, steady heat, soap films
Heat (parabolic) ut​=Δu smoothing, irreversible, infinite speed diffusion, Brownian motion, option pricing
Wave (hyperbolic) utt​=c2Δu propagation at speed c, reversible sound, light, vibrating strings

The Schrödinger equation iℏψt​=−2mℏ2​Δψ+Vψ looks like a heat equation with imaginary time and behaves like a wave equation: it is dispersive, with different frequencies travelling at different speeds.

Solving by eigenfunctions. Fourier's method: find the eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on the domain, Δϕk​=−λk​ϕk​, and expand. For the heat equation each mode simply decays, u=∑ck​e−λk​tϕk​, with high frequencies dying fastest, which is why heat flow smooths. For the wave equation each mode oscillates at frequency λk​​, and these are the overtones of a drum. Mark Kac asked in 1966 whether one can "hear the shape of a drum", that is, recover the domain from the λk​. Not always (Gordon, Webb, Wolpert, 1992), but the area and perimeter can be heard.

Fundamental solutions. The heat equation on Rn starting from a point source has the Gaussian solution (4πt)−n/2e−∣x∣2/4t, the density of Brownian motion. General solutions are convolutions with this kernel. The same idea, the Green's function, represents the solution of a linear PDE as an integral against the response to a point source.

GradModern PDE theory

Most PDEs of interest are nonlinear and have no formulas. The modern approach has three steps.

  1. Weaken the notion of solution. Multiply the equation by a smooth test function and integrate by parts, moving derivatives onto the test function. A function satisfying the resulting identity for all test functions is a weak solution. It need not be differentiable. Shock waves are weak solutions.
  2. Prove existence in a suitable function space, usually a Sobolev space Hs of functions with s derivatives in L2, using compactness or fixed-point arguments driven by a priori estimates: inequalities, typically from conserved or decreasing quantities like energy, that any solution must satisfy.
  3. Prove regularity and uniqueness: show the weak solution is in fact smooth, or understand its singularities.

For elliptic equations step 3 succeeds (elliptic regularity, and the De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory). For nonlinear evolution equations it is often the whole difficulty, and the governing idea is criticality: compare how the conserved quantities and the nonlinearity behave under rescaling. If the controlled quantity gets weaker at small scales the equation is supercritical and nothing prevents energy concentrating into a singularity.

In code Finite elements are weak solutions

The finite element method is step 1 made computational: restrict the weak formulation to a finite-dimensional space of piecewise polynomials on a mesh, and it becomes a sparse linear system. Lax–Milgram and Céa's lemma guarantee that the answer is the best approximation available in that space. Every structural, thermal and electromagnetic simulation package is running a theorem of functional analysis.

GradFluids

The Navier–Stokes equations for the velocity u and pressure p of an incompressible fluid with viscosity ν:

∂t​u+(u⋅∇)u=−∇p+νΔu,∇⋅u=0.

The term (u⋅∇)u says the fluid carries its own velocity along. It is what makes the equation nonlinear and produces turbulence. The viscous term νΔu smooths. With ν=0 they are the Euler equations. In two dimensions smooth solutions exist for all time. In three, Leray constructed global weak solutions in 1934, but whether smooth initial data stay smooth forever is unknown. The equation is supercritical: the energy bound is too weak to control small scales, where vortex stretching could in principle amplify without limit.

Theorem Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness (Millennium Problem)

Prove that smooth, finite-energy initial data in R3 always give a smooth solution for all time, or exhibit data whose solution develops a singularity in finite time.

Turbulence remains the great unsolved problem of classical physics. Kolmogorov's 1941 theory predicts by dimensional analysis that energy cascades from large eddies to small with a universal k−5/3 spectrum. Onsager's conjecture, that weak solutions of Euler conserve energy only if they are smoother than Hölder exponent 31​, was proved by Isett in 2018 using the convex integration technique of De Lellis and Székelyhidi, which builds wild solutions by adding ever-finer oscillations.

ResearchWhere research stands

Frontier From atoms to fluids: Hilbert's sixth problem

Hilbert asked in 1900 for a rigorous derivation of the laws of continuum physics from the mechanics of atoms. In 2025 Yu Deng, Zaher Hani and Xiao Ma carried out a long-sought step: starting from Newton's laws for a dilute gas of hard spheres, they derived Boltzmann's kinetic equation over long time intervals, and from it the equations of fluid dynamics. The earlier derivation by Lanford (1975) was valid only for a fraction of the average time between collisions. A subtle point is that Newton's laws are time-reversible and Boltzmann's equation is not, so the derivation must account for the origin of the arrow of time. Deng received a 2026 Fields Medal.

Frontier Blow-up, and a disputed announcement

Evidence had been accumulating that the Euler equations can develop singularities. Elgindi proved blow-up for rough initial data in 2019. Chen and Hou gave a computer-assisted proof for smooth data in a domain with boundary in 2022. In 2025 a group including Google DeepMind used machine-learning methods to find new families of unstable candidate singularities to high precision.

In August and September 2026 events moved fast. Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge announced an AI-assisted proof of singularity formation for the 3D Euler equations. On 8 September OpenAI announced that an internal AI system had produced a proof, with a formalisation in Lean, that a Navier–Stokes flow can blow up in finite time.

As of mid-November 2026 this is not a settled result. The construction uses a smooth external forcing term, which the Clay Institute's official problem statement permits in one of its variants but which many specialists regard as outside the spirit of the problem. The proof has not been peer reviewed, the Clay Institute still lists the problem as open and requires publication plus two years of scrutiny, and there is a public dispute over priority and credit. Treat it as a serious claim under examination.

Dispersive equations and solitons. Nonlinear Schrödinger and Korteweg–de Vries equations support solitons, solitary waves that pass through one another unchanged. The soliton resolution conjecture, that every solution eventually decomposes into solitons plus radiation, has been proved for some wave equations (Duyckaerts, Kenig, Merle and others). Deng and Hani's related work derives the wave kinetic equation, the foundation of wave turbulence theory.

Stochastic PDE. Equations driven by random noise are often too singular to make classical sense. Martin Hairer's regularity structures (Fields Medal 2014) gave meaning to the KPZ equation of interface growth and to equations of quantum field theory.

Smooth ergodic theory and homogeneous dynamics. Flows on spaces of lattices answer questions in number theory: Margulis proved the Oppenheim conjecture on values of quadratic forms this way, and the Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss theorem makes progress on the Littlewood conjecture. Mirzakhani and Eskin's "magic wand" theorem classifies orbit closures in moduli spaces of flat surfaces, with applications to billiards in polygons.

Machine learning for PDE. Neural operators and physics-informed networks approximate solution maps. For weather they now rival traditional solvers at a fraction of the compute. The mathematical theory of when and why they work is young.

History Poincaré's mistake

In 1889 Henri Poincaré won King Oscar II's prize for a memoir on the three-body problem. While it was being printed, a question from the editor led him to find a serious error: he had assumed certain curves could not cross. They can, forming an infinitely tangled web. He paid more than the prize money to have the print run destroyed. The corrected memoir contains the discovery of chaos.

Branches · Chapter 10 · about 19 min

Fourier Analysis and Hilbert Space

Decomposing functions into frequencies: Fourier series and transforms, sampling, uncertainty, operators and the mathematics of quantum mechanics.

In this chapter

CoreOne idea, used everywhere

In 1807 Joseph Fourier claimed that any periodic function is a sum of sines and cosines. The leading mathematicians of Paris objected that it could not be true, and the effort to decide who was right produced the modern definitions of function, integral, convergence and set. Fourier was essentially right.

The idea is linear algebra. Functions form a vector space. The functions einx are an orthonormal basis for it. They are also the eigenvectors of differentiation and of every translation-invariant operation, so in this basis differential equations become algebra and filters become multiplication. Every radio, every JPEG, every MRI scanner and every proof of the prime number theorem uses it.

CoreFourier series

Put the inner product ⟨f,g⟩=2π1​∫−ππ​f(x)g(x)​dx on functions of period 2π. The exponentials en​(x)=einx, for n∈Z, are orthonormal: ⟨en​,em​⟩ is 1 if n=m and 0 otherwise. The Fourier coefficients of f are its coordinates in this basis,

f^​(n)=⟨f,en​⟩=2π1​∫−ππ​f(x)e−inxdx,f(x)∼n=−∞∑∞​f^​(n)einx.

In what sense does the series converge to f? This is delicate, and the answers trace the history of analysis.

  • If f is continuously differentiable, the series converges uniformly.
  • There is a continuous function whose Fourier series diverges at a point (du Bois-Reymond, 1873).
  • For f∈L2 the series converges in the L2 norm (Riesz–Fischer, 1907), and it converges at almost every point (Carleson, 1966, a famously hard theorem).
  • There is an L1 function whose series diverges everywhere (Kolmogorov, 1926, aged 21).

Theorem Parseval

2π1​∫−ππ​∣f(x)∣2dx=n∑​​f^​(n)​2.

This is Pythagoras in infinitely many dimensions: energy in time equals energy in frequency. Applied to f(x)=x it gives Euler's ∑1/n2=π2/6.

Smoothness is decay. Since f′​(n)=inf^​(n), each derivative of f buys a factor 1/n of decay in the coefficients. A jump gives coefficients of size 1/n, a corner 1/n2, an analytic function exponential decay. This dictionary, between the regularity of a function and the size of its high frequencies, is what compression algorithms exploit and what PDE theory formalises as Sobolev spaces.

CoreThe Fourier transform

For functions on the whole line, sums over integer frequencies become integrals over all frequencies:

f^​(ξ)=∫−∞∞​f(x)e−2πixξdx,f(x)=∫−∞∞​f^​(ξ)e2πixξdξ.
In time or space In frequency
translate by a multiply by the phase e−2πiaξ
multiply by e2πibx (modulate) translate by b
differentiate multiply by 2πiξ
stretch by a factor λ compress by λ
convolve: (f∗g)(x)=∫f(y)g(x−y)dy multiply: f^​g^​
Gaussian e−πx2 the same Gaussian

The convolution theorem is the reason the transform matters in engineering. Any linear time-invariant system (a filter, an amplifier, a lens, a room's acoustics) acts by convolution with its impulse response, so in frequency it simply multiplies each frequency by a number. Plancherel's theorem, ∥f∥2​=​f^​​2​, says the transform is a rotation of the Hilbert space L2(R).

Application Sampling, aliasing and software radio

Shannon–Nyquist sampling theorem. If f^​ vanishes outside [−B,B], then f is completely determined by its samples at spacing 2B1​, and

f(t)=n∑​f(2Bn​)sinc(2Bt−n).

Sampling in time makes the spectrum periodic (this is the Poisson summation formula), so if the signal is not band-limited the copies overlap and high frequencies masquerade as low ones: aliasing.

A software-defined radio turns this into a design. It mixes the antenna signal with e−2πifc​t, which by the modulation rule shifts the band of interest down to zero frequency, low-pass filters, and samples the result as a complex signal: the I and Q channels are its real and imaginary parts. Complex samples at rate B capture a band of width B with no ambiguity between positive and negative frequencies. A waterfall display is the squared magnitude of a short-time Fourier transform. Narrow-band digital modes such as FT8 decode signals well below the audible noise floor because integrating over a long symbol concentrates signal energy into one frequency bin while noise spreads over all of them.

The uncertainty principle

Theorem Heisenberg's inequality

For f∈L2(R) with ∥f∥2​=1, the spread of ∣f∣2 about any point times the spread of ​f^​​2 about any point satisfies σx​σξ​≥4π1​, with equality only for Gaussians.

A function and its transform cannot both be sharply concentrated. A short pulse occupies a wide band, and a narrow filter rings for a long time. In quantum mechanics position and momentum wavefunctions are Fourier transforms of each other, and this inequality is the uncertainty principle. It is a theorem about functions, with no physics in it.

The discrete and fast transforms

On the cyclic group Z/N the Fourier transform is a finite sum, the DFT, an N×N unitary matrix. Computing it directly costs N2 operations. The fast Fourier transform (Cooley and Tukey, 1965, though Gauss had it in 1805) splits the sum into even and odd terms recursively and costs NlogN. That difference, between hours and milliseconds for realistic N, made digital signal processing possible. The same algorithm multiplies large integers and polynomials quickly, since multiplication of polynomials is convolution of coefficients. In 2019 Harvey and van der Hoeven used multidimensional FFTs to multiply n-bit integers in O(nlogn) time, conjecturally optimal.

GradHilbert space

A Hilbert space is a complete inner product space. Up to isomorphism there is only one that is infinite-dimensional and separable, ℓ2, the square-summable sequences, and L2 spaces are that same space in other coordinates. The geometry of finite-dimensional Euclidean space survives: orthogonal projection onto closed subspaces, orthonormal bases, and the Riesz representation theorem, that every continuous linear functional is an inner product with a fixed vector.

Linear maps are now called operators. Differentiation is an operator that is unbounded: it is defined only on a dense subspace and can make small functions large. An operator may have no eigenvectors: multiplication by x on L2[0,1] has none, though every λ∈[0,1] is "almost" an eigenvalue. The spectrum of T is the set of λ for which T−λ has no bounded inverse.

Theorem Spectral theorem

Every self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space is unitarily equivalent to multiplication by a real-valued function on some L2 space.

Diagonalisation survives, with a possibly continuous index in place of a finite list of eigenvalues. The Fourier transform is the unitary map that diagonalises differentiation.

Application The axioms of quantum mechanics

A state of a quantum system is a unit vector ψ in a Hilbert space. An observable is a self-adjoint operator A. Its spectrum is the set of possible measured values, and the spectral theorem supplies the probabilities. States evolve by the unitary group e−itH/ℏ generated by the energy operator H. Discrete spectrum means quantised energy levels, which is why atoms emit sharp spectral lines. Position and momentum are the operators "multiply by x" and "−iℏd/dx". They do not commute, and Heisenberg's inequality follows. Von Neumann set all this down in 1932, developing the theory of unbounded operators for the purpose.

Compact operators, the limits of finite-rank operators, behave like matrices: their spectrum is a sequence of eigenvalues tending to 0. Integral operators with reasonable kernels are compact, which is why the eigenfunction expansions of the previous chapter work, and why kernel methods in machine learning (Mercer's theorem) do too.

GradBeyond sines: wavelets and time–frequency analysis

Sines are perfectly localised in frequency and not at all in time. Real signals have transients. A wavelet basis consists of shifts and rescalings of one short oscillation, giving good localisation in both, with fine time resolution at high frequencies. Ingrid Daubechies constructed compactly supported orthonormal wavelets in 1988. JPEG 2000 uses them, and the multiscale idea returns in the convolution-and-pooling design of image networks.

Distributions make the transform work for objects that are not functions: the transform of the constant 1 is the delta function, and of a train of deltas another train of deltas.

GradHarmonic analysis on groups

Fourier series live on the circle, the transform on R, the DFT on Z/N. The common pattern: for any locally compact abelian group G, the continuous homomorphisms G→U(1) (the characters) form a dual group G^, and the Fourier transform is a unitary map from L2(G) to L2(G^). This is Pontryagin duality. Dirichlet's L-functions are Fourier analysis on (Z/n)×, and Tate's thesis derived the functional equation of zeta from Fourier analysis on the adeles, a group combining R with all the Qp​.

For non-abelian groups, characters are replaced by irreducible representations. The Peter–Weyl theorem decomposes L2 of a compact group. On the rotation group this gives spherical harmonics, the shapes of atomic orbitals and the basis used to analyse the cosmic microwave background. For non-compact groups such as SL2​(R) the theory (Harish-Chandra) is deep, and automorphic forms are its arithmetic refinement. The Langlands programme is, from this angle, non-abelian harmonic analysis.

ResearchWhere research stands

Restriction and Kakeya. Can the Fourier transform of an Lp function be meaningfully restricted to a curved surface such as a sphere? Stein's restriction conjecture predicts exactly for which p. It governs how solutions of the wave and Schrödinger equations disperse, and it implies the Kakeya conjecture from the analysis chapter. Methods introduced in the last fifteen years, polynomial partitioning (Guth) and decoupling (Bourgain and Demeter), solved long-standing problems including Vinogradov's mean value conjecture in number theory. After the 2025 proof of Kakeya in R3, Hong Wang and Shukun Wu have been developing a geometric route towards restriction itself.

A teenager's counterexample. The Mizohata–Takeuchi conjecture, a weighted restriction estimate proposed in the 1980s, was disproved in 2025 by Hannah Cairo, a 17-year-old who had taught herself much of the subject, by an explicit construction.

Sparse recovery. The uncertainty principle seems to forbid recovering a signal from few measurements. Compressed sensing shows that sparse signals are an exception, recoverable by convex optimisation from a number of random measurements proportional to their sparsity. The sparse Fourier transform computes the largest k coefficients in time nearly proportional to k.

Spectra of quasi-periodic operators. The almost Mathieu operator models an electron in a crystal under a magnetic field. Its spectrum, plotted against field strength, is the fractal "Hofstadter butterfly". That the spectrum is a Cantor set for every irrational parameter, the Ten Martini problem, was proved by Avila and Jitomirskaya in 2005. In 2025 Lingrui Ge, Jitomirskaya and collaborators extended such results to a broad class of operators with a more robust method.

Sphere packing by Fourier analysis. Viazovska's 2016 proof that the E8​ lattice gives the densest packing in dimension 8 constructs a "magic" function with prescribed signs for itself and its Fourier transform, built from modular forms. The same idea handled dimension 24. No other dimension above 3 is solved.

History Fourier's heat

Fourier developed his series to solve the heat equation, partly, it is said, from a preoccupation with warmth acquired on Napoleon's Egyptian expedition. Lagrange blocked publication for years over the lack of rigour. The book Théorie analytique de la chaleur appeared in 1822. Lord Kelvin called it a great mathematical poem. Dirichlet gave the first rigorous convergence proof in 1829 and, to do it, had to say for the first time what an arbitrary function is.

Branches · Chapter 11 · about 19 min

Probability and Statistics

Randomness made rigorous: limit theorems, Markov chains, martingales, Brownian motion, and how inference and information fit in.

In this chapter

CoreFrom gambling to measure theory

Probability began in 1654 with letters between Pascal and Fermat about dividing the stakes of an interrupted game. For three centuries it was a successful but philosophically muddled subject: what is a probability? In 1933 Kolmogorov cut the knot. Whatever probability means, its mathematics is measure theory with total mass 1. The interpretive arguments (frequency, degree of belief) continue, and the theorems do not depend on them.

Probability is now one of the most active areas of pure mathematics and the common language of statistics, physics, finance, genetics and machine learning.

CoreThe framework

Definition Probability space

A set Ω of outcomes, a σ-algebra F of events, and a measure P on F with P(Ω)=1. A random variable is a measurable function X:Ω→R. Its expectation is the Lebesgue integral E[X]=∫Ω​XdP.

The sample space Ω quickly recedes into the background. What matters is the distribution of X, the measure it induces on R, described by a mass function, a density, or in general the cumulative distribution function F(x)=P(X≤x). The variance is Var(X)=E[(X−EX)2].

Linearity of expectation, E[X+Y]=EX+EY, holds with no assumption of independence, and is absurdly powerful. The expected number of fixed points of a random permutation of n items is 1 for every n, because each item is fixed with probability 1/n, and there are n items.

Events are independent when P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). Conditional probability is P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), and rearranging gives

Theorem Bayes' rule

P(H∣D)=P(D)P(D∣H)P(H)​.

Example The base-rate effect

A condition affects 1 person in 1,000. A test detects it 99% of the time and gives a false positive 5% of the time. Given a positive result, the probability of having the condition is 0.99×0.001+0.05×0.9990.99×0.001​≈2%. The same arithmetic governs spam filters, alarm systems and any detector hunting a weak signal in noise: the threshold trades missed detections against false alarms, and the prior decides what a detection means.

A few distributions cover most needs: binomial (successes in n trials), Poisson (counts of rare events), geometric and exponential (waiting times, memoryless), normal or Gaussian (sums of many small effects), and for extremes and heavy tails the power laws, where the intuition trained on Gaussians fails badly.

CoreThe limit theorems

Let X1​,X2​,… be independent with the same distribution, mean μ and variance σ2, and let Sn​=X1​+⋯+Xn​.

Theorem Law of large numbers

Sn​/n→μ with probability 1.

Theorem Central limit theorem

σn​Sn​−nμ​⟶N(0,1)in distribution.

The law of large numbers is why averages are stable and casinos profitable. The central limit theorem says fluctuations around the average are of order n​ and have a universal shape, the bell curve, regardless of the distribution being summed. The details of the microscopic randomness wash out and only the mean and variance survive. Universality of this kind is the main theme of modern probability.

The proof idea is Fourier analysis. The characteristic function φX​(t)=E[eitX] is the Fourier transform of the distribution. Independence turns sums into products of characteristic functions, and a Taylor expansion shows the product converges to e−t2/2, the transform of the Gaussian.

How unlikely is a large deviation from the mean? Concentration inequalities answer with explicit bounds. Hoeffding: for independent variables in [0,1], P(∣Sn​/n−μ∣>t)≤2e−2nt2. Such bounds, not the asymptotic CLT, are what the analysis of randomised algorithms and of learning uses. Large deviation theory finds the exact exponential rate, given by an entropy.

CoreMarkov chains

A Markov chain is a random process whose next state depends only on its current state. It is described by a matrix P with Pij​ the probability of moving from i to j, and the distribution after n steps is the initial row vector times Pn.

Theorem Convergence

An irreducible, aperiodic chain on a finite state space has a unique stationary distribution π with πP=π, and from any start the distribution converges to π.

This is the Perron–Frobenius theorem of linear algebra, with π the left eigenvector for eigenvalue 1 and the speed of convergence set by the second-largest eigenvalue. PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random surfer.

Application Markov chain Monte Carlo

To sample from a complicated distribution π, such as a Bayesian posterior over a million parameters, design a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is π and run it. The Metropolis algorithm (1953) proposes a random move and accepts it with probability min(1,π(new)/π(old)), which needs π only up to a constant. The question of how long to run is the mixing time. Seven riffle shuffles are needed to mix a deck of 52 cards (Bayer and Diaconis), and the distance to uniform drops abruptly at that point, the cutoff phenomenon.

A simple random walk on the integer lattice Zd returns to its starting point with probability 1 in dimensions 1 and 2 and with probability less than 1 in dimension 3 and above (Pólya, 1921). A drunk man finds his way home, a drunk bird may not.

GradMartingales and Brownian motion

Graduate probability starts by defining conditional expectation E[X∣G] given a σ-algebra G of available information: the best prediction of X from that information, an orthogonal projection in L2.

Definition Martingale

A process (Mn​) with E[Mn+1​∣history up to n]=Mn​: a fair game.

The optional stopping theorem says no stopping strategy turns a fair game into a favourable one (under integrability conditions). The martingale convergence theorem says a bounded martingale converges. Martingale arguments give two-line solutions to problems such as gambler's ruin, and Azuma's inequality gives concentration for functions of many independent variables.

Brownian motion (Bt​)t≥0​ is the scaling limit of random walk: continuous paths, independent increments, and Bt​−Bs​ Gaussian with variance t−s. Einstein used it in 1905 to argue that atoms exist. Wiener constructed it rigorously in 1923 as a measure on the space of continuous functions. Its paths are continuous and nowhere differentiable, with fractal dimension 2 in the plane. Donsker's theorem is the CLT for whole paths: any random walk with finite variance, rescaled, converges to Brownian motion.

Stochastic calculus

Because Brownian paths have infinite length but finite quadratic variation, (dBt​)2=dt, calculus changes. Itô's formula, the chain rule for functions of Brownian motion, acquires a second-order term:

df(Bt​)=f′(Bt​)dBt​+21​f′′(Bt​)dt.

A stochastic differential equation dXt​=b(Xt​)dt+σ(Xt​)dBt​ describes a system with drift b and noise of strength σ. The density of Xt​ solves a PDE (the Fokker–Planck equation), and expectations of functionals of X solve another (the Feynman–Kac formula). Brownian motion is the probabilistic face of the heat equation: its transition density is the heat kernel, and harmonic functions are exactly those f for which f(Bt​) is a martingale.

Application Options and diffusion models

Black–Scholes (1973): model a stock price by dS=μSdt+σSdB. A portfolio holding the option and continuously rebalanced stock can be made riskless, and Itô's formula then forces the option price to solve a heat-type PDE. The price is an expectation under a changed probability measure in which the discounted stock is a martingale.

Diffusion models in generative AI run an SDE that gradually adds noise to data until it is pure Gaussian. A theorem of Anderson (1982) says the time-reversed process is also a diffusion, with a drift involving the gradient of the log-density, the score. A neural network is trained to estimate the score, and running the reverse SDE turns noise into images.

GradStatistics and information

Probability reasons from a model to data. Statistics inverts this. A frequentist estimates a fixed unknown parameter and reports procedures with guaranteed long-run error rates. The maximum likelihood estimator is asymptotically normal with variance given by the inverse Fisher information, and the Cramér–Rao bound says no unbiased estimator does better. A Bayesian puts a prior distribution on the parameter and updates by Bayes' rule. With enough data the two usually agree (Bernstein–von Mises).

High-dimensional statistics, with more parameters than observations, broke the classical theory and replaced it with one built on sparsity, regularisation (the lasso) and random matrix theory. The James–Stein paradox was the first sign: to estimate three or more unrelated means, shrinking all estimates towards a common point beats estimating each separately.

Information theory (Shannon, 1948) defines the entropy H(X)=−∑p(x)log2​p(x), the average number of bits needed to describe X. Shannon's source coding theorem says data cannot be compressed below its entropy. His channel coding theorem says every noisy channel has a capacity C such that reliable communication is possible at any rate below C and impossible above. For a channel of bandwidth W with Gaussian noise, C=Wlog2​(1+SNR). Codes that approach the limit (turbo, LDPC, polar) arrived only in the 1990s and 2000s. The Kullback–Leibler divergence measures the cost of using the wrong distribution, and minimising it is what "cross-entropy loss" does.

ResearchWhere research stands

Universality beyond Gaussians. Many growth processes, such as a burning front, a growing bacterial colony or a traffic model, have fluctuations of order t1/3, not t1/2, with a non-Gaussian limit law, the Tracy–Widom distribution, first found for the largest eigenvalue of a random matrix. This is the KPZ universality class. Its scaling limits, the KPZ fixed point (Matetski, Quastel, Remenik) and the directed landscape (Dauvergne, Ortmann, Virág), were constructed around 2018. Proving universality for general models is open.

Statistical mechanics. In percolation, each edge of a lattice is kept independently with probability p, and an infinite connected cluster appears above a critical value. Smirnov proved conformal invariance of critical percolation on the triangular lattice. Duminil-Copin's Fields Medal (2022) recognised a suite of results on the Ising and related models in dimensions 3 and 4. In August 2026 Quanta reported a proof that a broad class of networks has a sharp percolation transition, settling a question that had been open for decades.

Spin glasses and the geometry of high-dimensional randomness. Parisi's formula for the free energy of the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model, guessed by a non-rigorous "replica" method in 1979, was proved by Guerra and Talagrand in the 2000s. The same structures describe the loss landscapes of random optimisation problems and the thresholds at which random constraint-satisfaction problems become unsolvable or algorithmically hard.

Random geometry. Liouville quantum gravity and its equivalence to the Brownian map (Miller and Sheffield) give a canonical random surface. Schramm–Loewner evolution describes interfaces in two-dimensional critical models.

Random walks and algorithms. New techniques (spectral independence, entropy contraction) have given sharp mixing-time bounds for sampling algorithms and resolved conjectures on counting matroid bases. Shayan Oveis Gharan, a leader in this area, received the 2026 IMU Abacus Medal.

Statistical learning theory. Why do heavily over-parametrised neural networks generalise, contrary to classical bias–variance intuition? "Double descent" and benign overfitting are understood in linear and kernel models through random matrix theory. The general case is open and is among the most consequential questions in applied mathematics.

History Kolmogorov

Andrey Kolmogorov's 1933 monograph Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung, about sixty pages, gave the axioms used ever since. He was then 30 and had already built a function with a divergent Fourier series. He later founded the theory of turbulence scaling, algorithmic complexity (the length of the shortest program that prints a string), and with Arnold and Moser the KAM theory of the previous chapter.
