Branches · Chapter 12 · about 17 min

Combinatorics and Graph Theory

Counting, graphs, Ramsey theory and the probabilistic method: discrete mathematics, where problems are easy to state and proofs demand ingenuity.

In this chapter

CoreThe art of finite structures

Combinatorics studies finite, discrete objects: arrangements, graphs, set systems, codes. Its problems are often understandable in a minute and open for a century. For a long time the field was regarded as a collection of clever tricks. That changed in the second half of the twentieth century, largely through Paul Erdős, who posed thousands of problems and co-wrote papers with more than five hundred people, and through computer science, for which discrete mathematics is what calculus is to physics. Today it has deep general methods and some of the liveliest research in mathematics.

CoreCounting

The basic numbers: n! orderings of n objects, and (kn​)=k!(n−k)!n!​ ways to choose k of them. The best proofs in the subject are bijective: show two sets have the same size by pairing their elements. The identity (kn​)=(k−1n−1​)+(kn−1​) needs no algebra. A committee of k from n people either includes the oldest person or does not.

Inclusion–exclusion counts a union by alternately adding and subtracting intersections. It shows that the fraction of permutations with no fixed point tends to 1/e.

Generating functions encode a sequence a0​,a1​,a2​,… as the coefficients of a power series A(x)=∑an​xn. Combinatorial constructions become algebra: disjoint union is addition, forming pairs is multiplication, forming sequences is 1−A1​.

Example The Catalan numbers

Let cn​ count balanced strings of n pairs of parentheses. A nonempty balanced string is uniquely (A)B with A and B balanced, so C(x)=1+xC(x)2, and solving the quadratic gives

C(x)=2x1−1−4x​​,cn​=n+11​(n2n​)=1,1,2,5,14,42,…

The same numbers count binary trees with n nodes, triangulations of a polygon with n+2 sides, and some two hundred other families. The singularity of C(x) at x=41​ gives the growth rate cn​≈4n/(n3/2π​). Extracting asymptotics from the singularities of a generating function is analytic combinatorics, complex analysis in the service of counting and the basis for average-case analysis of algorithms.

The pigeonhole principle, that n+1 objects in n boxes force a shared box, sounds trivial and proves real theorems. Among any five points in a unit square, two are within 22​​. Any sequence of n2+1 distinct numbers has a monotone subsequence of length n+1 (Erdős–Szekeres).

CoreGraphs

A graph is a set of vertices with a set of edges joining pairs of them. It is the bare notion of a network.

  • Trees are connected graphs without cycles. A tree on n vertices has n−1 edges, and there are nn−2 labelled trees (Cayley).
  • Euler's formula V−E+F=2 holds for connected planar graphs. It implies that K5​ and K3,3​ are not planar, and Kuratowski's theorem says these two are the only obstructions.
  • Colouring. The chromatic number χ(G) is the fewest colours needed so that adjacent vertices differ. The four colour theorem (Appel and Haken, 1976) says planar graphs need at most four. It was the first major theorem proved with essential computer help, and it was formally verified in Coq in 2005.
  • Matchings. Hall's theorem: a bipartite graph has a matching covering one side iff every set of k vertices on that side has at least k neighbours. It is equivalent to max-flow min-cut and to linear programming duality.

Spectral graph theory studies a graph through the eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix or Laplacian. The second-smallest Laplacian eigenvalue measures how well connected the graph is (Cheeger's inequality) and how fast a random walk mixes. Expander graphs are sparse and yet highly connected. They are used to build error-correcting codes, derandomise algorithms and design robust networks. Their optimal versions, Ramanujan graphs, were first constructed using deep number theory.

CoreExtremal and Ramsey theory

Extremal combinatorics asks how large a structure can be while avoiding some pattern. Turán's theorem: a graph on n vertices with no triangle has at most n2/4 edges, achieved by the complete bipartite graph.

Ramsey theory says complete disorder is impossible.

Theorem Ramsey, 1930

For every k there is a number R(k) such that however the edges of the complete graph on R(k) vertices are coloured red and blue, some k vertices have all their edges the same colour.

R(3)=6 and R(4)=18. R(5) is known only to lie between 43 and 46. Erdős's joke: if aliens demand R(5) on pain of destruction, marshal every computer and mathematician. If they ask for R(6), try to destroy the aliens.

For large k, Erdős and Szekeres showed R(k)≤4k in 1935, and in 1947 Erdős proved R(k)≥2k/2 with an argument that founded a method.

Theorem The probabilistic method

To prove that an object with some property exists, show that a random object has it with positive probability.

Colour each edge of Kn​ by a fair coin. The expected number of single-coloured sets of k vertices is (kn​)21−(2k​), which is less than 1 when n=2k/2. So some colouring has none. Nobody knows an explicit colouring that comes close: finding hay in a haystack, in the standard phrase, is hard.

The Erdős–Rényi random graph G(n,p) shows phase transitions: properties that appear suddenly as p crosses a threshold. The giant component appears at p=1/n and connectivity at p=lnn/n. The mathematics is that of phase transitions in physics, and of epidemics, where the threshold is the reproduction number crossing 1.

GradStructure versus randomness

Theorem Szemerédi, 1975

Every set of integers with positive upper density contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.

Szemerédi's proof introduced the regularity lemma: every large graph can be partitioned into a bounded number of parts so that the edges between almost every pair of parts look random. Every large structure is a structured piece plus a pseudorandom piece plus a small error. That dichotomy now runs through combinatorics, number theory and theoretical computer science.

The theorem has four essentially different proofs: combinatorial (Szemerédi), ergodic-theoretic (Furstenberg), Fourier-analytic (Gowers, who introduced the uniformity norms that founded higher-order Fourier analysis) and via hypergraphs. Each opened a field.

Theorem Green and Tao, 2004

The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.

The primes have density zero, so Szemerédi does not apply directly. Green and Tao proved a version of the theorem relative to a pseudorandom host set and showed the primes sit densely inside one.

Additive combinatorics asks what a set A of integers must look like if its sumset A+A is small. Freiman's theorem: it must be a large piece of a generalised arithmetic progression. Quantitative versions matter greatly.

GradAlgebraic and geometric methods

The polynomial method. To bound the size of a set, find a low-degree polynomial vanishing on it and use algebra to derive a contradiction. Dvir's 2008 proof of the finite-field Kakeya conjecture is one page long. Guth and Katz used the method in 2010 to nearly solve Erdős's distinct distances problem: n points in the plane determine at least cn/logn distinct distances. In 2016 Croot, Lev and Pach, then Ellenberg and Gijswijt, used it to show that cap sets, subsets of F3n​ with no three points on a line, have size at most 2.756n, exponentially smaller than had been provable.

Linear algebra bounds. Associate vectors to the objects being counted and show they are linearly independent. The number of objects is then at most the dimension. Many extremal results about set systems are proved this way.

Error-correcting codes are packings in the Hamming cube {0,1}n: a set of codewords any two of which differ in at least d positions corrects ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors. Reed–Solomon codes, built from polynomials over finite fields, protect CDs, QR codes and deep-space links. Shannon proved good codes exist by the probabilistic method. Constructing them explicitly took fifty years.

ResearchWhere research stands

Ramsey numbers. In 2023 Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe proved R(k)≤(4−ε)k, the first exponential improvement on the 1935 upper bound. Follow-up work lowered the base further, to about 3.8. For off-diagonal numbers, Mattheus and Verstraëte determined the growth of R(4,t) up to logarithmic factors in 2023.

Arithmetic progressions. How large can a subset of {1,…,N} be with no three-term progression? In 2023 Kelley and Meka, two computer scientists, proved an upper bound of the form Nexp(−c(logN)1/12), a dramatic leap that nearly matches Behrend's 1946 construction. Also in 2023, Gowers, Green, Manners and Tao proved Marton's polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture in characteristic 2, and the proof was formalised in Lean within three weeks by an online collaboration, an early sign of what formalisation could do.

Erdős problems and AI. Thomas Bloom's website erdosproblems.com tracks more than a thousand problems posed by Erdős. Since late 2025 they have become the proving ground for AI in research mathematics. In May 2026 an OpenAI model disproved Erdős's 1946 unit distance conjecture, about how many pairs among n points in the plane can be exactly distance 1 apart, with an argument experts judged publishable in a top journal. A Google DeepMind paper in Science in October 2026 reported an agent that autonomously resolved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems it attempted, with every proof checked in Lean. The frontiers chapter gives the timeline.

Thresholds. The Kahn–Kalai conjecture, proved by Park and Pham in 2022 in a six-page paper, says that the threshold at which a structure appears in a random graph is within a logarithmic factor of a naive "expectation" guess.

Geometry. In 2023 David Smith, a hobbyist, discovered the "hat", a single tile that covers the plane but only non-periodically, solving the einstein problem. In 2024 Jineon Baek posted a claimed proof that Gerver's 1992 shape is the largest sofa that can be moved around a right-angled corridor corner. In high-dimensional sphere packing, lower bounds on density were improved in 2023 (by a logarithmic factor) and in 2025 by Boaz Klartag (by a factor of the dimension), the first large gains since 1947.

Human results of 2026. Quanta has reported this year a resolution of Graham's rearrangement conjecture (open 55 years), a new proof of the four colour theorem, and a proof of a long-conjectured "sandwich" theorem for graphs. Links are in the sources of the frontiers chapter.

History Erdős

Paul Erdős had no home and no job. He travelled with a suitcase from one collaborator to the next, announcing "my brain is open". He spoke of "The Book" in which God keeps the perfect proof of each theorem, and offered cash prizes for his problems, from 25 dollars to 10,000. A mathematician's Erdős number is the length of the shortest chain of co-authorships to him.

PreviousProbability and StatisticsNextAlgebraic Geometry

Branches · Chapter 13 · about 19 min

Algebraic Geometry

Shapes cut out by polynomial equations, from conic sections to schemes, and the dictionary between algebra and geometry that organises much of modern mathematics.

In this chapter

CoreEquations as shapes

Descartes' coordinates turned geometry into algebra: a circle is x2+y2=1. Algebraic geometry runs the dictionary in both directions for systems of polynomial equations in any number of variables, over any field. It has a reputation as the most abstract and technically demanding area of mathematics. It is also the place where number theory, complex analysis, topology and theoretical physics meet most often, which is why it gets a chapter in a guide that most undergraduate degrees would not give it.

Most bachelor's programmes touch it only through conics and perhaps elliptic curves, so this chapter moves quickly from a core you can reconstruct to ideas that are mostly graduate level.

CoreAffine varieties and the Nullstellensatz

Fix an algebraically closed field k, say C. An affine variety is the set of common zeros in kn of a collection of polynomials:

V(f1​,…,fm​)={x∈kn:f1​(x)=⋯=fm​(x)=0}.

Lines, conics, the cuspidal cubic y2=x3, the sphere, and the group SLn​ (matrices with det=1) are examples.

If f1​,…,fm​ vanish on a set, so does every combination ∑gi​fi​, so the natural algebraic object is the ideal I=(f1​,…,fm​) in k[x1​,…,xn​]. Conversely, to a set X one attaches the ideal I(X) of all polynomials vanishing on it.

Theorem Hilbert's Nullstellensatz

Over an algebraically closed field, I(V(J))=J​, the set of polynomials some power of which lies in J. In particular a system of polynomial equations has no solution iff 1 is a combination of the equations.

This sets up a perfect dictionary.

Geometry Algebra
variety X the ring k[X]=k[x1​,…,xn​]/I(X) of polynomial functions on X
point of X maximal ideal of k[X]
irreducible subvariety prime ideal
polynomial map X→Y ring homomorphism k[Y]→k[X] (backwards)
dimension length of the longest chain of prime ideals
X is smooth at p the local ring at p is regular

The geometry of X is entirely encoded in a commutative ring. That observation, pushed to its limit, is the idea of a scheme.

CoreProjective space and Bézout's theorem

Parallel lines do not meet, and that spoils clean statements. Projective space Pn adds points at infinity, one for each direction. Formally it is the set of lines through the origin in kn+1, with homogeneous coordinates [x0​:⋯:xn​] defined up to scaling. Varieties in Pn are cut out by homogeneous polynomials. Over C they are compact, which makes them far better behaved.

Theorem Bézout

Two plane curves of degrees d and e with no common component meet in exactly de points of P2, counted with multiplicity, over an algebraically closed field.

A line meets a conic in 2 points (possibly complex, possibly coincident when tangent). Two conics meet in 4. The theorem needs all three refinements, complex numbers, points at infinity and multiplicities, and each is a lesson in how to make a counting problem have a clean answer. Intersection theory generalises this, and enumerative geometry uses it: exactly 2 lines meet four general lines in space, a smooth cubic surface contains exactly 27 lines, and a general quintic threefold contains 2,875.

CoreCurves

A smooth projective curve over C is a compact Riemann surface, and its fundamental invariant is the genus g. A smooth plane curve of degree d has g=2(d−1)(d−2)​: lines and conics have genus 0, cubics genus 1.

The genus controls everything.

  • Genus 0: the curve is the projective line and can be parametrised by rational functions. The circle is parametrised by t↦(1+t21−t2​,1+t22t​), which generates all Pythagorean triples.
  • Genus 1: elliptic curves. No rational parametrisation, but a group law. Over C the curve is a torus C/Λ.
  • Genus ≥2: "general type". Over Q, only finitely many rational points (Faltings).

Here is the trichotomy of curvature from the uniformisation theorem (positive, zero, negative) reappearing as a trichotomy in arithmetic: infinitely many rational points with simple structure, a finitely generated group, finitely many. That geometry should govern arithmetic in this way is the guiding principle of Diophantine geometry.

Theorem Riemann–Roch

On a curve of genus g, the space L(D) of rational functions with poles bounded by a divisor D of degree d has dimension ℓ(D)=d−g+1+ℓ(K−D), where K is the canonical divisor. For d>2g−2 the last term vanishes.

Riemann–Roch counts how many functions exist with prescribed poles. It is the main tool for studying curves, and its generalisations (Hirzebruch, Grothendieck, Atiyah–Singer) are among the central theorems of twentieth-century mathematics.

Application Curves in engineering

Elliptic curve cryptography uses the group of points of an elliptic curve over a finite field. The best known attacks on its discrete logarithm problem are far slower than those on integers mod p, so keys are short. Algebraic geometry codes (Goppa) evaluate functions from L(D) at the points of a curve over Fq​, with Riemann–Roch giving the code's parameters. With curves having many points they beat the bound that random codes achieve. Pairings on elliptic curves underlie many zero-knowledge proof systems. Isogeny-based cryptography is a candidate for the post-quantum era, though one prominent scheme, SIDH, was broken in 2022 by a classical attack using abelian surfaces.

GradSheaves, cohomology and schemes

Between about 1955 and 1970 Alexander Grothendieck and his school rebuilt the subject. Three ideas carry it.

Sheaves. A sheaf assigns data, such as functions, to each open set of a space, with rules for restricting to smaller sets and gluing compatible local data. It is the precise tool for the local-to-global slogan. Sheaf cohomology Hi(X,F) measures the obstruction to gluing local sections into global ones.

Schemes. For any commutative ring R, define a space SpecR whose points are the prime ideals of R, and treat R as the ring of functions on it. For R=k[X] this recovers the variety X, with extra "generic" points. But now every ring is a space:

  • SpecZ is a "curve" whose points are the prime numbers. The integer n is a function on it whose "value" at p is nmodp.
  • A ring with nilpotent elements, such as k[x]/(x2), is a point with an infinitesimal tangent direction attached. Multiplicities and tangent vectors become honest geometric objects.
  • An equation with integer coefficients defines a scheme over SpecZ, a family of varieties, one over each finite field Fp​ and one over Q. Reduction mod p becomes restriction to a fibre.

Number theory becomes geometry. The analogy between number fields and function fields of curves, noted by Dedekind and Weber in the 1880s and treasured by Weil, becomes a common language.

Functorial thinking. A space is understood through the maps into it. A moduli space is one whose points classify geometric objects of some type: the moduli space Mg​ of curves of genus g has dimension 3g−3 for g≥2, a count Riemann knew. Constructing moduli spaces rigorously required stacks, which remember symmetries of the objects.

The Weil conjectures

For a variety X defined over Fq​, count its points over Fqn​ for each n and form a generating function, the zeta function of X. André Weil conjectured in 1949 that it is a rational function, satisfies a functional equation, has zeros and poles of absolute values q−i/2 (an analogue of the Riemann hypothesis), and that the degrees of its factors are the Betti numbers of the corresponding complex variety. The topology of the complex points controls counting over finite fields.

Grothendieck constructed étale cohomology to prove this, a cohomology theory that works over any field and behaves like the singular cohomology of topology. Deligne completed the proof of the Riemann hypothesis part in 1974. It remains the most convincing evidence for the classical Riemann hypothesis, and the model for what a proof might look like.

GradComplex algebraic geometry

Over C, analysis joins in. Hodge theory decomposes the cohomology of a smooth projective variety, Hk(X,C)=⨁p+q=k​Hp,q, using harmonic forms.

Theorem The Hodge conjecture (Millennium Problem)

On a smooth complex projective variety, every rational cohomology class of type (p,p) is a rational combination of classes of algebraic subvarieties.

It asks which topological cycles can be represented by algebraic equations. It is known for p=1 (Lefschetz) and in scattered cases.

Classification. Curves are classified by genus. Surfaces were classified by the Italian school and Kodaira. In dimension three and above the minimal model programme (Mori's Fields Medal, 1990, and Birkar, Cascini, Hacon and McKernan, 2006) seeks a simplest representative of each birational class, sorted by the positivity of the canonical bundle, which is the higher-dimensional version of the genus trichotomy.

Mirror symmetry. Physicists found in 1991 that counting rational curves on a quintic threefold, a formidable problem, could be done by computing periods of a different "mirror" manifold. The predicted numbers (2875,609250,317206375,…) were proved correct, and explaining the phenomenon has driven thirty years of work.

ResearchWhere research stands

Rational points. Faltings' theorem says curves of genus ≥2 have finitely many rational points but gives no way to find them. The Chabauty–Kim method has determined them for specific curves, including the "cursed curve" (2017). Lawrence and Venkatesh gave a new proof of Mordell's conjecture in 2018 through p-adic Hodge theory. Uniform bounds on the number of points, depending only on the genus and the rank, were proved by Dimitrov, Gao and Habegger in 2020. Faltings' 2026 Abel Prize honoured the foundations of all this.

Unlikely intersections and o-minimality. The 2026 Fields Medal to Jacob Tsimerman cited the André–Oort conjecture and results on period maps including a conjecture of Griffiths, all obtained by importing tame geometry from mathematical logic.

Rationality. Which varieties can be parametrised by rational functions? For smooth cubic hypersurfaces of dimension 4 the question was open for decades. In 2025 Katzarkov, Kontsevich, Pantev and Yu announced a proof that a very general cubic fourfold is not rational, using new invariants inspired by mirror symmetry and quantum cohomology. Experts are still digesting the argument.

New foundations. Derived algebraic geometry (Lurie, Toën, Vezzosi) builds homotopy theory into the definition of a space so that intersections always behave well. Prismatic cohomology (Bhatt and Scholze, 2019) unifies the various p-adic cohomology theories. Condensed mathematics aims to put analytic geometry over R, C and Qp​ on a single algebraic footing.

The Hodge conjecture. Among the results OpenAI released in October 2026 is a claimed proof for a special class, abelian varieties with complex multiplication. As of mid-November it had not been independently confirmed.

Computation. Numerical algebraic geometry solves polynomial systems by homotopy continuation, tracking solutions as an easy system is deformed into the hard one. It is used in robotics (the inverse kinematics of a general six-joint arm has 16 solutions), computer vision and chemical reaction networks. Tropical geometry replaces varieties with piecewise-linear shadows, turning some enumerative problems into combinatorics. It also describes the geometry of ReLU neural networks.

History Grothendieck

Alexander Grothendieck, stateless for most of his life, rewrote algebraic geometry in thousands of pages (EGA, SGA) at the IHÉS near Paris. He described his method as letting a rising sea soften a nut until it opens by itself: build the right general theory and the hard theorem becomes easy. He left the institute in 1970 over military funding, withdrew from mathematics, and spent his last decades in seclusion in the Pyrenees, leaving tens of thousands of pages of unpublished writing.

Mathematics Meets Computing · Chapter 14 · about 18 min

Computation, Logic and Categories

What can be computed, what can be computed efficiently, why proofs are programs, and the proof assistants now changing how mathematics is checked.

In this chapter

CoreThe chapter closest to your day job

Theoretical computer science is a branch of mathematics, and several of the deepest ideas of the last century came from asking what a computation is. This chapter covers three connected stories: computability (what is possible at all), complexity (what is feasible), and the correspondence between proofs and programs, which has turned into working software in the form of proof assistants. Category theory appears along the way as the shared language.

CoreComputability

In 1936 Alan Turing defined a simple abstract machine, a finite controller reading and writing symbols on an unbounded tape, and argued that it captures everything that can be computed by following rules. Church's lambda calculus and Gödel's recursive functions, defined independently, compute exactly the same functions. The Church–Turing thesis is the claim that this class is the computable functions. Every programming language you have used is equivalent to it.

Theorem The halting problem is undecidable

There is no program that takes an arbitrary program and input and decides whether it eventually halts.

The proof is Cantor's diagonal argument. Suppose halts(p, x) existed. Define

def paradox(p):
    if halts(p, p):
        while True: pass   # loop forever
    return                 # otherwise halt

Does paradox(paradox) halt? If it does, it loops. If it loops, it halts. So halts cannot exist.

Rice's theorem generalises: every nontrivial question about the behaviour of programs is undecidable. No static analyser can be both sound and complete. Undecidability then spreads by reduction to problems that do not mention programs at all:

  • whether a polynomial equation with integer coefficients has an integer solution (Hilbert's tenth problem; Matiyasevich, 1970, building on Davis, Putnam and Robinson);
  • whether two finitely presented groups are isomorphic, or whether a word in the generators is the identity;
  • whether a given set of tiles can tile the plane;
  • whether two 4-manifolds are homeomorphic.

Going deeper Busy beavers

Let BB(n) be the largest number of steps an n-state Turing machine can run before halting. BB grows faster than any computable function, because knowing it would solve the halting problem. BB(4)=107. In 2024 an online collaboration proved BB(5)=47,176,870 by classifying every 5-state machine, with the proof checked in the Coq proof assistant. BB(6) is at least a tower of exponentials too tall to write down, and settling it would require resolving a Collatz-like number theory problem. There is an explicit machine with 745 states whose halting is independent of ZFC: Gödel's theorem with a concrete size.

CoreComplexity

Among computable problems, which are feasibly computable? P is the class of yes/no problems solvable in time polynomial in the input length. NP is the class for which a proposed solution can be checked in polynomial time: a Sudoku is hard to solve and easy to verify.

Theorem P versus NP (Millennium Problem)

Is every problem whose solutions can be verified quickly also solvable quickly? Almost everyone believes P=NP. Nobody can prove it.

Cook and Levin showed in 1971 that satisfiability of Boolean formulas (SAT) is NP-complete: every problem in NP reduces to it. Karp added 21 more in 1972, and thousands are now known, including travelling salesman, graph colouring, integer programming and protein threading. They are all the same problem in different clothes. Either all have fast algorithms or none do.

Why is it so hard to prove? Three barrier theorems (relativisation, natural proofs, algebrisation) show that whole families of proof techniques cannot separate P from NP. The natural proofs barrier is notable: a proof of the common kind would yield an algorithm that breaks the cryptography we believe secure.

Randomness and proofs. Three surprises from the theory:

  • Randomness may not help. Under plausible hardness assumptions every efficient randomised algorithm can be derandomised. Primality testing, long the standard example of the power of randomness, was shown to be in P in 2002 (Agrawal, Kayal, Saxena).
  • Zero-knowledge proofs. You can convince someone that a statement is true while revealing nothing else. Everything in NP has such a proof, given one-way functions. This is now deployed in blockchains and privacy systems.
  • The PCP theorem. Every NP proof can be rewritten so that a verifier who reads only a constant number of randomly chosen bits catches any error with high probability. Equivalently, for many optimisation problems even approximate solutions are NP-hard.

Quantum computing. A quantum computer manipulates a unit vector in (C2)⊗n by unitary matrices. Shor's algorithm factors integers in polynomial time by using the quantum Fourier transform to find the period of axmodN. It is believed that quantum computers cannot solve NP-complete problems efficiently.

GradProofs are programs

Theorem The Curry–Howard correspondence

Propositions correspond to types, and proofs correspond to programs. Checking a proof is type-checking.

Logic Programming
proposition A type A
proof of A value of type A
A⇒B function type A -> B
A∧B pair type (A, B)
A∨B tagged union Either A B
false the empty type
∀x∈A, P(x) dependent function: given x, returns a value of type P x
∃x∈A, P(x) dependent pair: a value x with a proof of P x
proof by induction structural recursion

A proof of A⇒B is a function turning evidence for A into evidence for B. Modus ponens is function application. To make this cover all of mathematics the type system needs dependent types, types that mention values, such as "vectors of length n" or "proofs that n is prime". Per Martin-Löf's type theory and the Calculus of Constructions supply them, and they are the foundations of the proof assistants Coq (now Rocq), Agda and Lean.

In code What a formal proof looks like

In Lean 4, with the community library Mathlib:

theorem infinitude_of_primes (n : ℕ) : ∃ p, n ≤ p ∧ Nat.Prime p := by
  let p := Nat.minFac (n ! + 1)
  have hp : Nat.Prime p := Nat.minFac_prime (by
    have := Nat.factorial_pos n; omega)
  refine ⟨p, ?_, hp⟩
  by_contra h
  have h1 : p ∣ n ! := Nat.dvd_factorial hp.pos (by omega)
  have h2 : p ∣ 1 := (Nat.dvd_add_right h1).mp (Nat.minFac_dvd _)
  exact hp.one_lt.ne' (Nat.dvd_one.mp h2)

This is Euclid's argument: take the smallest prime factor p of n!+1. If p were below n it would divide n!, hence divide 1. The words after by are tactics, small programs that build the proof term. A small trusted kernel checks the result. The exact lemma names drift between Mathlib versions, so treat this as illustrative. If it compiles, the theorem is true, with no referee needed.

Mathlib had well over a million lines covering most of an undergraduate curriculum and a good deal of graduate mathematics by 2025. Milestones in formalisation: the four colour theorem (2005), the Feit–Thompson odd order theorem (2012), the Kepler conjecture on sphere packing (2014, whose human referees had given up after years), Scholze's liquid tensor experiment (2022), the polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture (2023), and in 2026 Fermat's Last Theorem.

GradCategory theory

Eilenberg and Mac Lane introduced categories in 1945 to make precise the word "natural". The definitions are short.

Definition Category, functor, natural transformation

A category has objects, and arrows (morphisms) between objects that compose associatively, with an identity arrow on each object. A functor F:C→D sends objects to objects and arrows to arrows, preserving composition and identities. A natural transformation between functors F,G is a family of arrows F(X)→G(X) compatible with every arrow X→Y.

Sets and functions, groups and homomorphisms, spaces and continuous maps are categories. So is any partial order, any single group (one object, with elements as arrows), and the types and functions of a programming language. The fundamental group and homology are functors from spaces to groups, which is why they can be used to prove maps do not exist.

Category theory characterises constructions by universal properties: by how they relate to everything else, not by how they are built. The product A×B is the object such that a map into it is the same as a pair of maps into A and B. That one definition gives Cartesian products of sets, direct products of groups, product topologies, greatest lower bounds in an order, and pair types.

Adjunctions capture "best approximate inverse". The free group on a set is left adjoint to the forgetful functor from groups to sets. Currying, the bijection between functions A×B→C and A→(B→C), is an adjunction. In logic, ∃ and ∀ are the left and right adjoints of substitution.

Theorem Yoneda lemma

An object is determined, up to unique isomorphism, by the collection of all arrows into it. More precisely, natural transformations from Hom(−,A) to a functor F correspond to elements of F(A).

An object is its relationships. Grothendieck's geometry, with spaces defined by the maps into them, is the Yoneda lemma taken seriously.

In code Monads

A monad is a functor T with natural transformations unit : A -> T A and join : T (T A) -> T A satisfying associativity and identity laws. List, Option, Future and State are monads, and flatMap is join after map. They arose in algebra, where the monad of an adjunction describes "algebras" such as groups and rings uniformly. Moggi noticed in 1989 that they also model computational effects, and Haskell made them famous.

Homotopy type theory reads a type as a space, a term as a point and a proof of equality as a path, so that there can be many different proofs that two things are equal, with paths between those. Voevodsky's univalence axiom says equivalent types are equal, formalising the practice of treating isomorphic structures as the same.

ResearchWhere research stands

Circuit lower bounds and the meaning of hardness. We cannot rule out that SAT has linear-size circuits. Meta-complexity studies the difficulty of determining difficulty (the minimum circuit size problem) and has connected it tightly to the existence of one-way functions (Liu and Pass, 2020).

Space is more powerful than time. In 2025 Ryan Williams proved that any computation running in time t can be simulated using only about tlogt​ memory, a large improvement on a fifty-year-old result, using a surprising algorithm for evaluating trees with reused memory.

Hardness of approximation. Subhash Khot's unique games conjecture (2002) would pin down exactly how well many NP-hard problems can be approximated. The related 2-to-2 games theorem was proved in 2018. Quanta reported in October 2026 a further milestone by Dor Minzer and students, posted in haste amid rumours of an AI proof of the full conjecture.

Quantum complexity. MIP∗=RE (Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, Yuen, 2020): a verifier talking to two entangled provers can check answers to the halting problem. The result also refuted the Connes embedding conjecture in operator algebras, a problem from pure analysis solved by complexity theory.

Formalisation at scale. In September 2026 Anthropic announced that its Claude models, working largely autonomously for eleven days, had produced the first complete machine-checked proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean, about 13 million lines, building on Mathlib and on the human FLT project at Imperial College. Kevin Buzzard, who leads that project, reviewed it. Auto-formalisation of the existing research literature now looks like an engineering project. What that means for how mathematics is refereed, taught and trusted is being argued about in real time, and the next chapter but one returns to it.

History Turing and von Neumann

Turing wrote "On computable numbers" at 23 to settle Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem, the question of whether there is a mechanical procedure to decide mathematical truth. To show there is none he first had to define "mechanical procedure", and so invented the stored-program computer on paper a decade before one was built. Gödel wrote to von Neumann in 1956 asking, in effect, whether P equals NP. The letter was found decades later.

Mathematics Meets Computing · Chapter 15 · about 17 min

Numerical Analysis, Optimisation and Learning

How continuous mathematics is actually computed: floating point, conditioning, iterative methods, convex optimisation, and the mathematics inside machine learning.

In this chapter

CoreMathematics that has to run

Pure mathematics proves a solution exists. Applied mathematics has to produce it, to a stated accuracy, in finite time, on a machine that cannot represent most real numbers. That constraint generates deep mathematics of its own. The algorithms in this chapter are the most executed pieces of mathematics on Earth: they run inside every simulation, every optimiser, every trained model.

CoreFloating point and conditioning

An IEEE double stores a sign, an 11-bit exponent and 52 bits of mantissa, about 16 decimal digits. Floating-point numbers are a finite set, dense near zero and sparse far out. Arithmetic rounds to the nearest representable number, so it is not associative, and 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3.

Two different things can go wrong in a computation, and separating them is the first idea of numerical analysis.

Definition Conditioning and stability

The condition number of a problem measures how much its answer changes when the input is perturbed. It is a property of the mathematics. Stability is a property of an algorithm: it is backward stable if the answer it returns is the exact answer to a slightly perturbed input.

A backward stable algorithm applied to a well-conditioned problem gives an accurate answer. Nothing can rescue an ill-conditioned problem. For solving Ax=b the condition number is κ(A)=σmax​/σmin​, and you lose about log10​κ digits. Subtracting nearly equal numbers (catastrophic cancellation) is the classic way an algorithm creates ill-conditioning the problem did not have. The textbook quadratic formula does it when b2≫4ac.

Example Wilkinson's polynomial

The polynomial (x−1)(x−2)⋯(x−20) has roots 1,…,20. Change the coefficient of x19 from −210 to −210−2−23 and several roots move far into the complex plane, with imaginary parts near 3. Roots can be astronomically sensitive to coefficients. The lesson James Wilkinson drew: never compute eigenvalues by forming the characteristic polynomial.

CoreThe core algorithms

Linear systems. Gaussian elimination is the factorisation A=LU, costing about 32​n3 operations. With partial pivoting it is stable in practice. Symmetric positive definite systems use Cholesky, least squares uses QR, and rank-deficient problems use the SVD. For the huge sparse systems that come from discretised PDEs, direct methods are too costly, and iterative methods take over. The conjugate gradient method finds the best approximation in the Krylov subspace spanned by b,Ab,A2b,… and needs only the ability to multiply by A. Its convergence depends on κ​, so the practical art is preconditioning. Multigrid methods solve some PDE systems in time proportional to the number of unknowns.

Eigenvalues. By Abel and Galois there is no formula for the roots of a polynomial of degree five or more, so every eigenvalue algorithm must iterate. The QR algorithm (Francis and Kublanovskaya, 1961) repeatedly factors and remultiplies in reverse order. It converges cubically for symmetric matrices and is among the most successful algorithms ever designed.

Nonlinear equations. Newton's method xk+1​=xk​−f(xk​)/f′(xk​) linearises and solves. Near a simple root it converges quadratically, doubling the number of correct digits at each step. Far from a root it may do anything, and the regions of starting points converging to each root are fractal.

Interpolation and approximation. High-degree polynomial interpolation at equally spaced points oscillates wildly near the ends (the Runge phenomenon). At Chebyshev points, which cluster near the ends, it converges rapidly for smooth functions. Chebyshev expansions are Fourier series in disguise under x=cosθ, so the FFT computes them.

Quadrature. Gaussian quadrature chooses n nodes and weights to integrate polynomials of degree 2n−1 exactly. In high dimensions grids are hopeless: 10 points per axis in 100 dimensions is 10100 points. Monte Carlo integration has error O(N−1/2) regardless of dimension, which is why randomness is indispensable in high-dimensional computation.

Differential equations. Time-stepping methods (Runge–Kutta, multistep) trade accuracy against stability. Stiff problems, with widely separated time scales, force implicit methods. For PDEs the Lax equivalence theorem says a consistent scheme converges iff it is stable, and the CFL condition bounds the time step by the mesh size over the wave speed. Symplectic integrators preserve the geometry of Hamiltonian systems and keep simulated planets in orbit for billions of years where generic methods spiral.

CoreOptimisation

Minimise f(x) subject to constraints. The dividing line between easy and hard is convexity, not linearity.

Definition Convex

A set is convex if it contains the segment between any two of its points. A function is convex if its graph lies below its chords: f(tx+(1−t)y)≤tf(x)+(1−t)f(y).

Convex problems can be solved reliably and efficiently at large scale. Linear programming, optimising a linear function over a polyhedron, is the central case. The simplex method (Dantzig, 1947) walks along vertices. Interior-point methods (Karmarkar, 1984) cut through the middle and run in polynomial time.

Duality. Every convex problem has a dual problem whose optimal value bounds the original from the other side, and under mild conditions the two agree. Lagrange multipliers are the dual variables, and they have a meaning: the price of relaxing each constraint. Max-flow equals min-cut, and the minimax theorem of game theory, are both duality.

Gradient descent xk+1​=xk​−η∇f(xk​) needs about κ iterations for a function with condition number κ. Nesterov's accelerated method needs only κ​, and that is optimal among first-order methods. Second-order (Newton) methods converge faster per step and cost more per step.

Application Control and estimation

The Kalman filter (1960) estimates the state of a linear system from noisy measurements, optimally for Gaussian noise. It is recursive least squares with a dynamics model, alternating a predict step with a Bayesian update. It navigated Apollo and runs in every GPS receiver and phone. Its dual, the linear-quadratic regulator, computes optimal feedback control by solving a matrix Riccati equation. Model-predictive control solves a convex optimisation problem at every time step, in real time.

GradThe mathematics of machine learning

Training a neural network is minimising a non-convex function of billions of variables by a noisy first-order method, and it works far better than classical theory predicts. The ingredients are all in earlier chapters.

  • Backpropagation is the chain rule evaluated in reverse order, as the geometry chapter described. Its cost is a small constant multiple of evaluating the function.
  • Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a random sample of the data. The noise is a feature: it biases the search towards wide, flat minima.
  • Expressivity. Universal approximation theorems say that networks can approximate any continuous function. They do not say why they do it with few parameters. For functions with compositional structure, depth gives exponential savings over width.
  • Generalisation. Classical learning theory (VC dimension, Rademacher complexity) bounds test error by training error plus a complexity term, and predicts that models with more parameters than data should overfit. They do not. In the limit of infinite width, training is equivalent to kernel regression with the neural tangent kernel. Real networks learn features, which that limit does not capture.
  • Attention. A transformer layer computes, for each token, a weighted average of all tokens' value vectors, with weights from a softmax of inner products: softmax(QKT/d​)V. It is linear algebra, one nonlinearity, and a great deal of data.

The curse and blessing of dimensionality. In high dimensions volume concentrates in strange places. Nearly all of a ball's volume is near its surface, and two random unit vectors are nearly orthogonal. So neighbourhood-based methods fail. The same phenomenon, concentration of measure, makes random projections preserve distances (the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma: n points embed in O(logn/ε2) dimensions with distortion 1±ε), which is why sketching, hashing and compressed sensing work.

Inverse problems. Recovering a cause from an effect, such as an image from a CT scan or a subsurface from seismic echoes, is typically ill-posed: small data errors produce large errors in the answer. Regularisation restores stability by adding prior information, a penalty on roughness or on non-sparsity. Tikhonov regularisation, the lasso and the Bayesian prior are the same idea.

GradMathematical physics

The oldest branch of applied mathematics supplies the newest pure mathematics. Statistical mechanics derives macroscopic behaviour from microscopic randomness, and its renormalisation group explains why different systems share the same critical exponents. Quantum field theory, the framework of particle physics, makes predictions verified to twelve decimal places and still has no complete rigorous definition in four dimensions. That gap is the Yang–Mills Millennium Problem. Physicists' non-rigorous manipulations of path integrals have repeatedly predicted correct, deep theorems in geometry and topology (mirror symmetry, Seiberg–Witten invariants, knot invariants), and explaining why is a research programme in itself.

ResearchWhere research stands

Proving theorems with computers and intervals. Interval arithmetic computes with guaranteed error bounds, so a numerical computation can be a proof. The Lorenz attractor, the Kepler conjecture and recent blow-up results for fluid equations rely on it. The 2025 and 2026 work on singularities combined neural-network searches for approximate solutions with rigorous computer-assisted verification.

Faster linear algebra and optimisation. A decade of work produced almost-linear-time algorithms for Laplacian systems and, in 2022, for maximum flow (Chen, Kyng, Liu, Peng, Probst Gutenberg and Sachdeva), by combining interior-point methods with dynamic graph data structures.

Theory of deep learning. Open questions include why SGD finds generalising solutions, how and when networks learn features, what in-context learning in transformers computes, and whether training dynamics can be predicted. Mechanistic interpretability, reverse-engineering the algorithms a trained network implements, leans on linear algebra and sparse coding. Singular learning theory applies algebraic geometry to the degenerate geometry of loss landscapes.

Sampling and transport. Diffusion models and flow matching connect to optimal transport and to Schrödinger bridges. Sharp guarantees for sampling from non-log-concave distributions are being developed.

Scientific machine learning. Learned surrogates now forecast weather at operational quality and predict protein structure (AlphaFold, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024). Combining them with the conservation laws and symmetries of the underlying equations, and quantifying their uncertainty, is an open field with obvious stakes.

AI as a tool for mathematics itself. Systems such as AlphaEvolve search for mathematical constructions (better bounds, new algorithms) by evolving programs. That, and the theorem-proving systems of 2026, are the subject of the next chapter.

History Von Neumann and Goldstine, Turing, Wilkinson

Numerical analysis as a discipline dates from the 1940s, when von Neumann and Goldstine, and independently Turing, analysed rounding errors in Gaussian elimination for the first electronic computers. Their bounds were so pessimistic that large systems looked unsolvable. Wilkinson's backward error analysis in the 1950s showed that the algorithm is far better than the bounds suggested, and in the process found the right question to ask.

Now · Chapter 16 · about 22 min

The Frontier in 2026

Prizes, proofs and the open problems as they stand in mid-November 2026, a year in which the practice of research mathematics changed faster than in any in living memory.

In this chapter

How to read this chapter

Everything here is dated. It was written in mid-November 2026 from public sources, which are listed at the end. Results are marked by how far they have been checked:

  • Established: published or widely verified by specialists.
  • Announced: a preprint or public claim that experts take seriously and are still checking.
  • Disputed: a claim whose correctness, scope or attribution is being argued over.

If you left mathematics in 2010 you return to a subject in which the big structural programmes continued roughly as expected, a string of famous problems fell to human mathematicians between 2013 and 2025, and then, over about eighteen months, machines began producing research-level proofs. This chapter takes those in turn.

ResearchThe prizes of 2026

Abel Prize: Gerd Faltings (Max Planck Institute for Mathematics, Bonn), "for introducing powerful tools in arithmetic geometry and resolving longstanding diophantine conjectures of Mordell and Lang". His 1983 proof of the Mordell conjecture, that a curve of genus at least 2 has finitely many rational points, was the event that made arithmetic geometry the centre of number theory. He is the first German laureate.

Fields Medals, awarded on 23 July at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia, the first Congress in the United States since 1986:

Medallist Field For
Yu Deng (Chicago) PDE deriving Boltzmann's equation from hard-sphere dynamics, and wave kinetic equations from dispersive systems
John Pardon (Stony Brook) symplectic geometry, topology virtual fundamental cycles, Fukaya categories, counting holomorphic curves, and work on 3-manifolds and knots
Jacob Tsimerman (Toronto) arithmetic geometry making o-minimality a basic method, with proofs of André–Oort and a conjecture of Griffiths
Hong Wang (NYU and IHES) harmonic analysis the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions, and results on Furstenberg sets and Falconer's distance problem

Hong Wang is the third woman to receive the medal, after Maryam Mirzakhani (2014) and Maryna Viazovska (2022). At the same ceremony the Abacus Medal for mathematical aspects of computer science went to Shayan Oveis Gharan, the Chern Medal for lifetime achievement to Graeme Segal, and the Leelavati Prize for public outreach to Hannah Fry.

All four medals are for work in the classical style: long papers by one to three authors solving problems that had resisted the best people for decades. Each connects to an earlier chapter: Deng to differential equations, Pardon to topology and geometry, Tsimerman to foundations and algebraic geometry, Wang to analysis and Fourier analysis.

ResearchA decade and a half of human results

A selective list of what you missed, with the chapter where each is explained.

Year Result Chapter
2013 Bounded gaps between primes (Zhang; then Maynard, Tao, Polymath) Number theory
2013 Kadison–Singer problem (Marcus, Spielman, Srivastava) Linear algebra

ResearchThe machines arrive

The run-up

Until 2024, AI's contributions to mathematics were of two kinds: specialised search (AlphaTensor finding matrix multiplication schemes, machine-learned hints for knot invariants) and language models that were unreliable at anything beyond textbook problems. In July 2024 DeepMind's AlphaProof, which writes proofs in Lean so that every step is machine-checked, reached silver-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad. A year later systems from two labs reached gold.

Olympiad problems are hard but have known solutions. The shift to open problems came at the end of 2025, on the list of problems left by Paul Erdős. Terence Tao kept a public record. By mid-January 2026 about fifteen had moved from open to solved, most of them with AI involvement and some autonomously, typically with a language model producing an argument and a second tool translating it into Lean. Many of these were at the easy end. A fair number of claimed solutions turned out to be rediscoveries of forgotten papers. In April, Quanta's survey of the field quoted Tao saying that 2025 was when the tools became useful for many different tasks.

May to November 2026

The unit distance problem (Established). On 20 May OpenAI announced that one of its general-purpose models had disproved a conjecture Erdős made in 1946 about the maximum number of pairs of points at distance exactly 1 among n points in the plane. Mathematicians who read the paper said they would have accepted it for a leading journal. It was the first AI result of that standing.

The Jacobian conjecture (Established). On 20 July Levent Alpöge, a number theorist at Anthropic and Harvard, posted a counterexample to the 1939 Jacobian conjecture in three variables, found with Claude Fable 5 during the World Cup final. The whole counterexample is a formula 216 characters long. The next section checks it.

Euler and Navier–Stokes (Announced, and Disputed). In mid-August Tristan Buckmaster (NYU) and Alpöge announced an AI-assisted proof that solutions of the 3D Euler equations can blow up. On 8 September OpenAI announced that an internal system, running about 10,000 coordinated agents for 88 hours, had proved finite-time blow-up for Navier–Stokes with a Lean formalisation. Three objections followed. The construction uses an external force, permitted by one variant of the official Millennium Problem statement and regarded by many specialists as not the real question. Buckmaster, whose Euler result came first, publicly disputed OpenAI's account of priority and credit. And nothing has been refereed. The Clay Mathematics Institute's president called the announcement exciting and said evaluation would be unhurried and rigorous. The Institute still lists the problem as unsolved.

Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean (Established). On 4 September Anthropic released a complete formal proof of Fermat's Last Theorem: about 13 million lines of Lean written by Claude agents in eleven days, depending only on Lean's three standard axioms and checked by independent kernels. Kevin Buzzard, whose human project had expected to need years more, reviewed the statement and the result. This is not a new proof. It is Wiles's proof, and the large body of mathematics underneath it, translated into a form a computer can verify. In November the company said the same job could now be done in 30 hours.

The October release (Announced). On 6 October OpenAI published a repository of several hundred AI-written results, about a third with formal proofs and, in its own words, at different stages of verification. One stood out: a proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, that none has a zero with real part above 87​, which also excludes Landau–Siegel zeros. Number theorists have since rewritten parts of the argument in their own words, and Quanta reported in mid-October that experts largely believe the shorter of the two proofs. The same release contained a claimed case of the Hodge conjecture, not yet confirmed.

Systematic evaluation (Established). A DeepMind paper published in Science in October measured what one such system can do: of 353 open Erdős problems attempted, the agent resolved 9, and of 492 open conjectures from the OEIS it proved 44, all checked in Lean. A success rate of a few percent on problems selected for being open is a useful calibration against the headlines.

ResearchCheck one yourself

A counterexample is the friendliest kind of theorem: you do not need to know how it was found to know it is right. The claim is that this polynomial map F:C3→C3 has constant nonzero Jacobian determinant and is not injective.

from sympy import symbols, Matrix, expand

x, y, z = symbols("x y z")
F = Matrix([
    (1 + x*y)**3 * z + y**2 * (1 + x*y) * (4 + 3*x*y),
    y + 3*x*(1 + x*y)**2 * z + 3*x*y**2 * (4 + 3*x*y),
    2*x - 3*x**2*y - x**3*z,
])

print(expand(F.jacobian([x, y, z]).det()))        # -2

for p in [(-1, 2, 8), (0, 2, -16), (1, -1, 5)]:
    print(p, list(F.subs(dict(zip((x, y, z), p)))))  # [0, 2, 0] each time

I ran this while writing the guide. The determinant expands to the constant −2, and the three integer points (−1,2,8), (0,2,−16) and (1,−1,5) all map to (0,2,0). A map that sends three points to one has no inverse. So a problem open for 87 years, with a long history of wrong proofs, is refuted by twenty lines of Python.

Two things are worth noticing. The example is small enough that it could in principle have been found by a determined search decades ago, and nobody found it, in part because most people expected the conjecture to be true. And verifying it teaches you nothing about why it exists. The two-variable case, the one Keller originally asked about, remains open, and whatever structure makes dimension 3 fail has yet to be understood.

ResearchWhat has and has not changed

Checking has become cheap. A formal proof in Lean is correct if the statement says what you think it says. That last clause carries weight: a theorem can be formalised with a subtly wrong definition, and the scope argument over Navier–Stokes is about exactly which statement was proved. But the bottleneck of refereeing, which left the Kepler conjecture in limbo for years and the abc claim unresolved for more than a decade, is dissolving.

Finding has become cheaper for some kinds of problem. The clearest AI successes are counterexamples, constructions, and proofs that combine known techniques across areas no single person has mastered. Whether the systems can create the kind of new theory that Grothendieck or Thurston created is not known. No Fields-level body of work has come from one.

Understanding is still the point, and is not automatic. Thurston wrote that the product of mathematics is human understanding, with theorems as a by-product. A 13-million-line proof or a 216-character counterexample certifies a fact without explaining it. Much of the human work since October has been exactly this: rewriting machine proofs until people can see why they work.

The community is divided. A Quanta feature in October asked whether this is the end of mathematics as its practitioners know it, and reported grief and anger alongside excitement. Some mathematicians have called for a boycott of AI for proving new theorems. Others, Tao prominent among them, describe a future of large collaborative projects in which people set direction and machines handle detail. Arguments about credit, about the role of companies whose models and prompts are private, and about how to train students are unresolved.

For a returning student the practical consequences are good ones. Proof assistants give instant feedback on your own arguments. Language models are capable tutors for standard material, provided you check what they say. And knowing the mathematics matters more than before, because stating the right theorem, judging whether a result is interesting, and understanding an answer are the parts that have not been automated.

ResearchThe Millennium Problems today

Problem Status in November 2026
Poincaré conjecture Proved (Perelman, 2003). The only one resolved under the prize rules.
Riemann hypothesis Open. A zero-free half-plane Res>87​ has been announced and is being verified.
P versus NP Open, with no credible approach.
Navier–Stokes Officially open. A disputed AI-generated blow-up proof for the forced equation was announced in September 2026.
Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Open. Known for analytic rank 0 and 1.
Hodge conjecture Open. A special case (CM abelian varieties) was claimed in October 2026.
Yang–Mills and the mass gap Open.

ResearchProblems still standing

A sample of questions that remain open, each stateable in a sentence.

  • Twin primes: infinitely many primes p with p+2 prime? Goldbach: is every even number above 2 a sum of two primes?
  • Collatz: does iterating n↦n/2 (even) or 3n+1 (odd) always reach 1?
  • The Jacobian conjecture in two variables.
  • Kakeya in dimension four and above, and the restriction conjecture.
  • Is ω=2? Can n×n matrices be multiplied in about n2 steps?
  • The smooth Poincaré conjecture in dimension four: is there an exotic 4-sphere?
  • The abc conjecture, and bounded ranks of elliptic curves.
  • Diagonal Ramsey numbers: does R(k)1/k converge, and to what?
  • The Langlands correspondence for number fields.
  • Is the Mandelbrot set locally connected?
  • Do one-way functions exist? Is BPP=P?
  • Why does deep learning generalise?

Any of these may look different by the time you read this. That is the news of 2026.

Now · Chapter 17 · about 13 min

Where to Go Next

Books, lectures and projects for going deeper, with routes that suit someone who already programs.

In this chapter

Choosing a direction

You now have a map. The next step is to pick one region and read a real book on it, slowly, with a pencil. Reading mathematics is unlike reading anything else. A page an hour is a normal pace. The test of understanding is whether you can reproduce the proof of a theorem the next day without looking, and whether you can say what goes wrong when each hypothesis is dropped.

Three pieces of advice from people who returned to mathematics after a long gap:

  • Rebuild the trunk first. Linear algebra and analysis are used by everything else. A month on each pays for itself many times over.
  • Prefer one book finished to five started. Pick by taste, then stay.
  • Compute. You have an advantage most students lack. Whenever a definition is new, write code that produces examples. Whenever a theorem surprises you, test it numerically.

CoreBooks for the core

These are widely used, well-written and suitable for self-study.

Subject A gentle start The standard next step
Proof and language Velleman, How to Prove It Aigner and Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK (for pleasure)
Linear algebra Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right Trefethen and Bau, Numerical Linear Algebra
Real analysis Abbott, Understanding Analysis Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis; Tao, Analysis I and II
Complex analysis Needham, Visual Complex Analysis Stein and Shakarchi, Complex Analysis
Abstract algebra Pinter, A Book of Abstract Algebra Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra; Aluffi, Algebra: Chapter 0
Topology Munkres, Topology Hatcher, Algebraic Topology (free online)
Number theory Silverman, A Friendly Introduction to Number Theory Ireland and Rosen, A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory
Probability Blitzstein and Hwang, Introduction to Probability Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples (free online)
Differential equations Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos Evans, Partial Differential Equations
Combinatorics Graham, Knuth and Patashnik, Concrete Mathematics Alon and Spencer, The Probabilistic Method

The four-volume Princeton Lectures in Analysis by Stein and Shakarchi (Fourier analysis, complex analysis, real analysis, functional analysis) is the best single path through analysis from undergraduate to graduate level, and begins with Fourier series for motivation.

GradBooks for the graduate layer

  • Geometry: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, then Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds. Tu, An Introduction to Manifolds is shorter. Needham, Visual Differential Geometry and Forms for intuition.
  • Algebraic geometry: Reid, Undergraduate Algebraic Geometry; Fulton, Algebraic Curves (free online); then Vakil, The Rising Sea (free online), which is written to be read alone.
  • Algebraic number theory and elliptic curves: Stewart and Tall, Algebraic Number Theory and Fermat's Last Theorem; Silverman and Tate, Rational Points on Elliptic Curves; then Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves.
  • Representation theory: Fulton and Harris, Representation Theory: A First Course; Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups.
  • Measure and functional analysis: Axler, Measure, Integration and Real Analysis (free online); Folland, Real Analysis.
  • Logic and set theory: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic; Kunen, Set Theory.
  • Category theory: Riehl, Category Theory in Context (free online); Leinster, Basic Category Theory (free online). For programmers, Milewski, Category Theory for Programmers.
  • Complexity: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation; Arora and Barak, Computational Complexity; Wigderson, Mathematics and Computation (free online), a panoramic view.
  • High-dimensional probability and learning: Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability (free online); Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (free online).
  • Information theory: MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (free online); Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory.
  • Mathematical physics: Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics; Penrose, The Road to Reality as a tour of the whole landscape.

One reference deserves a line of its own: The Princeton Companion to Mathematics, edited by Timothy Gowers. It is a thousand pages of essays by leading mathematicians explaining their fields to each other, and it is the book this guide would most like to be.

CoreLectures and reading online

  • MIT OpenCourseWare: Strang's linear algebra (18.06) remains the standard. The real analysis, algebra and topology sequences have full notes and videos.
  • 3Blue1Brown: Grant Sanderson's Essence of Linear Algebra and Essence of Calculus series rebuild intuition quickly. His videos on Fourier transforms, the zeta function and group theory match chapters here.
  • Richard Borcherds (Fields Medal 1998) has recorded complete graduate courses on YouTube: group theory, Galois theory, algebraic geometry, number theory, Lie groups.
  • Quanta Magazine for research news written for non-specialists, with accurate mathematics.
  • Terence Tao's blog for expository posts at every level and running commentary on the use of AI in research.
  • arXiv (arxiv.org, section math) for the papers themselves. Start with surveys: search for "survey", "introduction to" or Bourbaki seminar and ICM proceedings articles, which are written to be read by outsiders.
  • The ICM 2026 lectures, including the laudations explaining each Fields medallist's work, are on the Simons Foundation and IMU channels.

GradProjects for a programmer

Reading is half of it. These projects use skills you already have, and each one forces contact with real mathematics.

Learn Lean. Install Lean 4 and work through the Natural Number Game in a browser, then Mathematics in Lean (free online). Proving that 2​ is irrational, or Lagrange's theorem, in a proof assistant is the nearest thing to having a patient examiner check every step. Then formalise a small theorem from a chapter of this guide. Mathlib welcomes contributions and its Zulip chat is friendly to newcomers. After the events of 2026 this is also the best vantage point for understanding where the field is heading.

Experiment with SageMath or SymPy. Compute class groups of quadratic fields and look for patterns. Count points on elliptic curves mod p and plot ap​/2p​ to see the Sato–Tate distribution emerge. Compute zeros of ζ with mpmath and histogram their normalised spacings against the random-matrix prediction.

Signal processing from first principles. Implement the FFT. Write a polyphase channeliser or a matched filter and measure the processing gain you derived on paper. Decode a real signal: demodulating a recorded narrow-band transmission from raw I/Q samples exercises complex exponentials, filtering, sampling theory and detection statistics in a single afternoon.

Numerical experiments in dynamics. Integrate the three-body problem with a symplectic integrator and with Runge–Kutta, and compare energy drift. Compute Lyapunov exponents. Render Julia sets and Newton fractals. Simulate percolation and the Ising model and locate the phase transition.

Topology of data. Run persistent homology (Ripser, GUDHI) on a point cloud you care about and learn to read the barcode.

Build a small autodiff engine, forward and reverse mode, and connect it to the pushforward and pullback of the geometry chapter. Then implement a tiny transformer on top of it.

Open problems you can touch. The Collatz conjecture, Ramsey numbers and many Erdős problems (erdosproblems.com) invite computational exploration. OEIS, the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, is the first place to check whether a sequence you computed is known. Contributions from programmers are common: the busy beaver collaboration that proved BB(5) was mostly volunteers writing code.

CoreSuggested routes through this guide

  • If physics and astronomy are the pull: Linear algebra → Analysis → Fourier → Differential equations → Geometry (to general relativity) → Topology. Then Arnold, and Lee's manifolds books, then a text on general relativity such as Carroll or Wald.
  • If signals and information are the pull: Linear algebra → Fourier → Probability → Applied → Complex analysis. Then Stein and Shakarchi's first volume, MacKay, and Oppenheim and Schafer for the engineering view.
  • If computation and logic are the pull: Language → Foundations → Computation → Combinatorics → Algebra. Then Sipser, Lean, and Riehl.
  • If pure mathematics for its own sake is the pull: Algebra → Number theory → Complex analysis → Algebraic geometry → Topology. The proof of Fermat's Last Theorem is a worthy ten-year target. Many people have set out on it for fun.

A closing thought

G. H. Hardy wrote that a mathematician, like a painter or a poet, is a maker of patterns, and that the patterns must be beautiful. The subject you studied in 2010 is still that. It is also, this year, in the middle of the largest change to its working methods since the invention of the journal. It is a good time to come back.
